entry.title: SAP AI Adoption & Learning Week – Day 2 in review
entry.content:
In my Day 1 recap, I talked about the gap between AI investment and AI value, and closed with the ambition that the organizations that lead won't just automate what exists, they will reinvent it. Day 2 was where that ambition got concrete, showing what reinvention looks like in Finance, Customer Experience, and Supply Chain, and giving consultants a practical session on getting SAP Joule for Consultants running on live projects.

Here's my recap of the day's sessions and the questions that came up most.

AI is everywhere. Results aren't.

That was the opening line of the Day 2 Morning Briefing (recording), and it set the tone for everything that followed. 74% of organizations are stuck in pilot and the reason is structural: generic AI lacks business context, point solutions create patchwork, and building without governance slows everything down. Most enterprises are still assembling AI function by function, a copilot here, a point solution there. Each adds intelligence to a silo. None of them talk to each other.

SAP's answer is one system. The SAP Autonomous Suite is organized around five domains, Finance, Spend, Supply Chain, HR, and Customer Experience, where people direct, Assistants coordinate, and Agents execute. Domains move as one: a decision in Finance shows up in Supply Chain; a change in demand triggers a response in Procurement. Industry AI extends each domain with vertical knowledge and regulatory logic from day one. Explore all Joule Assistants here.

On Day 1, we looked at Joule Work as the unified workspace where this all comes together. Day 2 went deeper, showing what the Autonomous Enterprise means for Finance, CX, and Supply Chain specifically. The sessions that followed answered exactly that. Rewatch them:

  • From SAP Sapphire to What's Next in Finance: See how a billing process map changes when agents take over the work that shouldn't need a person (recording).
  • From SAP Sapphire to What's Next in Supply Chain Management: Get a sneak peek of the Asset and Service Assistant (recording).
  • From SAP Sapphire to What's Next in Customer Experience: See how CX becomes a revenue function by closing the disconnect between engagement data and business outcomes (recording).

Seeing what the Autonomous Enterprise looks like in each domain is the first step. Getting there is the next. The day's final session was built for the consultants and partners doing that work. Two features released at SAP Sapphire 2026 were the headline of this session, and both are already available:

Custom Knowledge Grounding connects SAP Joule for Consultants to your organization's own content such as project files, internal knowledge repositories, delivery standards, and policies indexed via SAP AI Core Grounding. The result: answers that draw on SAP's full knowledge base and your firm's institutional knowledge at the same time. Less time searching. Responses that reflect how your organization actually works.

  • SAP Joule for Consultants Custom Knowledge Grounding
  • Enhance SAP Joule for Consultants with Custom Knowledge Grounding

Expert Workspace enables persistent personalization in SAP Joule for Consultants by introducing reusable Experts with custom instructions and file-based grounding. It is a centralized environment within the SAP Joule for Consultants console where users can create, configure, and manage Experts at design time. Experts can then be explicitly activated during conversations at run time.

  • SAP Joule for Consultants Expert Workspace
  • Getting Started with SAP Joule for Consultants Expert Workspace

Rewatch From Activation to Application: Getting Started with SAP Joule for Consultants.

Before I wrap up, I wanted to address the questions that came up most:

  • What does it actually cost?
    SAP Joule for Consultants is a premium AI feature.     Pricing is user-based, reflecting scenarios where value is directly tied to individual productivity. It is offered as a Per User Per Month package, with a fixed number of 35 AI Units per user. Consumption is tracked in SAP for Me. Find out more in the Whitepaper Understanding the SAP Business AI Commercial Model.
  • What are the prerequisites for activating SAP Joule for Consultants?
    As a customer or partner, you will need to have AI Units and a SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) Global Account. There are no other technical dependencies and no system requirements. SAP Joule for Consultants is a standalone web-based assistant, which means on-premise, ECC, and private cloud customers can activate and use it just as easily as public cloud customers. Find out how to enable SAP Joule for Consultants in the Discovery Center Mission.

Day 1 set the foundation. Day 2 put it into practice. Continue with the full series:

entry.title: One Controlling Area by Design: Why SAP Made This Choice for the Public Cloud
entry.content:
Introduction

If you have been part of an SAP implementation, working as a CO consultant, you have almost certainly sat in a workshop where someone asked: "How many controlling areas should we use?" .  What followed was rarely a short conversation. Teams debated regional autonomy, currency configurations, chart of accounts alignment, fiscal calendars, and organisational boundaries; often for hours, sometimes for days. The difficulty? The controlling area has no equivalent in the real business world. It is a SAP system construct, not an organisational entity. Yet it consumed disproportionate design energy in project after project.

SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Public Edition resolves this by design: exactly one controlling area. This is not a limitation, it is a deliberate architectural choice that simplifies implementation, enables consistent analytics, and reduces total cost of ownership. Critically, it does not prevent you from meeting regional requirements for currencies or deviating fiscal calendars. It just changes how you meet them, in a cleaner, more maintainable way.

 

The Controlling Area Debate - An Artificial Problem

In SAP on-premise or private cloud, the controlling area is the second highest-level organisational unit in Controlling. It determines the fiscal year variant, chart of accounts, and CO currency settings (group currency). Company codes are assigned to a controlling area, and all assigned entities must share the same settings.

This setup leads to a recurring design question in implementations: should you create one controlling area for the whole enterprise, or separate ones per region, country group, or business unit? Arguments on both sides have been made countless times:

The fundamental issue is that the controlling area was designed many years back, for SAP products with less functionality. In a unified, cloud-delivered system with embedded analytics and continuous innovation delivery, its structural purpose largely disappears. The debate around it is a symptom of mapping an on-premise design pattern to a cloud reality where it no longer fits.

 

Why SAP Chose One Controlling Area for the Public Cloud

1. Fit-to-Standard and Lifecycle Stability

S/4HANA Cloud, Public Edition is a fit-to-standard solution. SAP pushes new innovations on a regular basis to all tenants simultaneously. Every additional degree of structural variance, such as multiple controlling areas, increases the surface area for regression, conflict, and manual remediation during upgrades. One controlling area directly reduces this risk and keeps the solution upgrade-safe across its entire lifecycle.

2. Consistent Embedded Analytics and the Universal Journal

The Universal Journal (table ACDOCA) is the single source of truth for all financial and controlling postings. Embedded analytics, Margin Analysis, and group-wide reports rely on harmonised organisational and currency settings to deliver consistent results without additional transformation layers. A single controlling area guarantees that fiscal periods, currency types, and organisational hierarchies are aligned across all entities from the moment of go-live.

3. End-to-End CO Integrity Supports Intercompany Processes

Cost allocation methods like for example universal allocations, direct activity allocations, and settlements all operate within the boundaries of a controlling area. With one controlling area, these processes run seamlessly across all company codes. There are no cross-area gaps, no reconciliation interfaces, and no manual period-alignment steps.

Intercompany cost flows work uniformly when all entities share one controlling area. The alternative, routing costs across controlling area boundaries, requires workarounds that increase data complexity and audit risk.

 

Benefits of One Controlling Area

  • Faster time to value: Fewer structural decisions in the design phase means quicker, cleaner implementations.
  • Unified CO processes: Universal allocations, activity allocation, and settlement work across all entities without gaps or workarounds.
  • Consistent analytics out of the box: All embedded reports and Margin Analysis work consistently across all company codes from day one.
  • Lower TCO: Reduced configuration variance, less testing effort, and lower risk during upgrades.
  • Future-ready with UPA: Universal Parallel Accounting enables full regional requirements (currencies, fiscal calendars) without structural duplication.
  • No unproductive design debates: Teams focus on business process design rather than system architecture choices that do not reflect real organisational boundaries.

 

Requirement 1 — Regional Currency Reporting

A common concern is: "We need management reporting in USD for our US entities and EUR for our European entities. Doesn't that require separate controlling areas?"

It does not. Within one controlling area, the enhanced currency concept addresses both local and managerial reporting needs simultaneously.

 

 

Practical Recommendation

The company code currency is already predefined in the system and is the national currency of the company code (e.g. USD for US entities and EUR for many European entities). You can use the additional freely defined currency to setup a second currency that plays the role of the group currency. One setup option could be to use group currency (USD) for enterprise-level views. European managers could then get EUR from the freely defined currency; US managers get USD from the group currency. Group and freely defined currency can of course also be defined vice versa (group = EUR and freely defined = USD).
No separate controlling area is required.

Requirement 2 - Deviating Fiscal Year Variants with Universal Parallel Accounting

Another common requirement: "Our Asia Pacific entities operate on an Apr–Mar fiscal year. Surely that requires its own controlling area?"
Not in S/4HANA Cloud, Public Edition - and the reason is Universal Parallel Accounting (UPA).

Universal Parallel Accounting - Always Active

UPA is not an optional add-on in the public cloud. It is always on. Its core principle is that every Financial Accounting (FI) and Controlling (CO) posting is written simultaneously and completely to all configured ledgers. Period-end processes, including for example allocations, settlements, WIP calculations, FX valuations, and balance carryforward, execute per ledger and respect each ledger's own fiscal calendar. This is the fundamental architectural enabler that makes deviating fiscal years possible within a single controlling area.

 

How the Setup Works

 

What "Fully Parallel" Means in Practice

Because UPA writes every posting to all ledgers simultaneously, APAC entities have complete, real-time data in both 0L and L1 at all times. There is no batch replication, no reconciliation between ledgers, and no separate posting step. CO allocations, overhead settlements, WIP/variance calculations, and so on can be executed per ledger, using the correct fiscal periods for each calendar. This is not a workaround: it is the intended operating model.

 

Putting It All Together — A Design Blueprint

The following configuration pattern addresses both the currency and fiscal year requirements described in this post within a single controlling area in S/4HANA Cloud, Public Edition. Currencies and fiscal year variants are just examples, the configuration can look different for different companies:

 

Conclusion

The controlling area is one of those SAP concepts that accumulated enormous design weight over decades of on-premise implementations. It is a system organising principle that has no direct equivalent in the real business world. The debates it generated in projects were often expensive, contentious, and ultimately inconclusive.

SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Public Edition makes a clear architectural statement: one controlling area, always. This is not a restriction on business capability, it is a simplification of implementation complexity. Requirements that justified multiple controlling areas (regional currencies, deviating fiscal calendars, managerial reporting boundaries) can be addressed within this single controlling area design using the tools that are provided with Universal Parallel Accounting: parallel ledgers and additional currency types.

The result is a system that is easier to implement, easier to operate, easier to upgrade, and more analytically consistent - without sacrificing any of the regional and statutory requirements that real businesses need to meet.

entry.title: The Invoice Already Knows the SAP PO. Artificial Intelligence Finds the Right Line.
entry.content:
The Problem: A Month-End Nightmare

While working with an accounts payable team, I watched month-end turn into a nightmare in a PO-based MIRO world. Every open supplier invoice has to post before the books close, and leadership watches blocked and unmatched invoices like a Canis-Lupus.

So as the SAP specialist lead on the ground, I dug in. Turns out a big chunk of those stuck invoices had nothing to do with price or qty variance. They simply had no safe way to match invoice lines to PO line items  the invoice didn't mirror the PO's structure, the vendor never referenced PO line numbers, and SAP had nothing to propose a clean match from.

So it fell to a person. Invoice open on one screen, MIRO on the other, manually mapping every line to the right PO or GR before the system would even let it through. Multiply that by a stack of invoices at month-end, and a "standard" process turns into a grind nobody signed up for.

ChatGPT-Prompt: Can you please generate image for The Problem: A Month-End Nightmare in e-Invoice to post in SAP MIRO where SAP PO based Invoice 2 PO Matching line items.

The Invoice Already Knows the PO. Just Not the Line.

Here's the thing nobody outside AP really understands about this problem: the invoice does tell you which PO it belongs to. UBL 2.1 and Peppol BIS 3.0 e-invoices carry the PO reference right there in the header 

<cac:OrderReference>PO-4500067890</cac:OrderReference> 
(OR)
<cbc:BuyerReference>PO-4500067890</cbc:BuyerReference>

So SAP knows the invoice is against PO-4500067890.

What it doesn't know is which of the dozens of lines across those three POs each invoice line actually maps to. That mapping only exists at the header level. Line-level PO references are technically possible in the standard  I've seen maybe one vendor in the wild actually populate them. Everyone else leaves you to figure it out.

And "figure it out" usually means a human, squinting at two descriptions:

Invoice says

PO says

Hex Bolts M10

Hex Head Bolt M10x50mm Grade 8.8

Office Paper A4 500 sheets

A4 Copy Paper Ream 500

Same item. Zero words in common that matter. A junior AP clerk gets this right in about two seconds. A rules engine built on exact-match or Levenshtein distance gets it wrong every time, because the problem was never spelling  it's meaning.

  • Live demo: https://heisenberglupenix-invmatchmaker.hf.space/

Why Not Just Call an LLM?

The obvious answer today is "just call an LLM." It would probably match "Hex Bolts M10" to "Hex Head Bolt M10x50mm Grade 8.8" just fine if you asked it nicely. But an LLM call per invoice line, multiplied by every candidate PO line, across every invoice a company processes in a month, is slow and expensive for what is fundamentally a narrow, repetitive, high-volume matching task  not a reasoning task. You don't need something that can write you a poem to know two part descriptions refer to the same bolt.

Traditional machine learning doesn't get the hype right now. But for "does this invoice line mean the same thing as this PO line," it's the right tool, not the consolation prize.

The Practical Approach

The knowledge I picked up from University of Auckland's (Artificial Intelligence, Masters course) and Stanford's (Machine Learning course) pointed me toward a Feature-Based Ranking Model (FBRM) approach. This isn't a full AP automation suite there are enough of those already, and most are still doing header-level three-way match dressed up as "AI." I built specifically the part that's missing: given an invoice and the POs it already references, which PO line does each invoice line belong to.

Technical deep dive (skip ahead to "Why This Instead of Buying Off the Shelf" if you're not into the Machine Learning details)

Sentence-BERT (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, pre-trained, no fine-tuning yet) encodes both descriptions into 384-dimension vectors and takes the cosine similarity. That alone gets you most of the way "Hex Bolts M10" and "Hex Head Bolt M10x50mm Grade 8.8" land close together in embedding space even though they share almost no substring.

But semantic similarity alone isn't enough to post against, so I layer eight features on top of it per invoice/PO-line pair:

Created the pipleline to set the weights for Feature-Based Ranking Model. 

Weighted sum, blended 40/60 with the raw semantic score, clipped to [0,1]. Top-k (k=3) candidates per invoice line, greedy conflict resolution so two invoice lines don't both claim the same PO line, then triage:

What's Still a Prototype (Being Upfront)

That weighted scorer is a stand-in. I'm calling it "LightGBM" in the docs because that's what it becomes in the next phase, but right now it's a fixed weight vector I hand-tuned against a handful of sample invoices not a model trained on labelled data. If you've read anything I've written before, you know I don't like shipping something and letting the framing overstate what it actually does. This is proof that the shape of the solution works, not a claim that the numbers above are production-grade.

Step 1: Semantic Encoding

  • SentenceTransformer converts invoice and PO descriptions into numerical embeddings.
  • Captures semantic meaning beyond exact text matching.

Step 2: Similarity Calculation

  • Cosine Similarity measures the semantic closeness between invoice and PO embeddings.
  • Produces a similarity score used as the foundation for candidate matching.

Example:

1.0 = very similar meaning
0.0 = unrelated meaning
-1.0 = opposite meaning
Step 3: Build Feature Vectors
  • Every Invoice-PO combination receives 8 features.
  • F0, F1, F2 ....... F8 features are hand-picked. 

Step 4: Rank the match and select Top-K

  • Combine all evidence into one match score.
  • Tok-K: Stright cut to K=3 values from the combined matching scores.

Step-5: Conflict Resolution:

  • Prevent multiple invoice lines claiming the same PO line.

Step-6: Apply Triage 

  • ≥ 90% → auto-suggested, safe to post without a human touching it
  • 60–89% → goes to a reviewer, with the top-3 candidates shown so they're picking, not typing
  • < 60% → manual resolution  the AI is telling you honestly that it doesn't know

The honest next step is the same one I took with the SAP ticket classifier I wrote about a few weeks back: get real labelled pairs actual accept/override/reject decisions from an AP team, or anonymized MIRO history and train an actual ranker on them instead of a vector I picked by eye. Everything else (the SAP MM field alignment, the INVOIC02 IDoc output, the triage thresholds) is close to done. The learning is the part that's still owed.

You can check the fine-tuined sap-ticket-classifier-bert from the collections. mentioned in the below image.  

 

Why This Instead of Buying Something Off the Shelf

Most AP automation platforms are strong at OCR and header-level tolerance checks, and I have no interest in reinventing that. What they're largely missing is the line-level semantic layer sitting between those two things. Rossum's PO-matching extension, for example, matches line items by ID and field overlap  not by what they actually mean.

That's the space this fills: not a capture tool, not a three-way match engine, just the component that resolves "which line," once "which PO" is already settled at the header.

Try It

If your team is still doing this matching by hand and you're curious what a semantic-first approach looks like on real SAP MM fields, the MVP is live invoice XML in, SAP-ready IDoc XML out, and Concur ready JSON, CSV file nothing hidden behind a demo request form.

Live demo and docs linked below. This is a Phase 1 MVP feedback on where it breaks is genuinely more useful to me than praise.

SAP-Invoice-To-PO-LineMatching: https://huggingface.co/spaces/HeisenbergLupenix/SAP-Invoice-To-PO-LineMatching

Author: If you find this information helpful, please consider clicking the "Like" button on this blog and sharing your thoughts in the comments section below. You can also connect with the author on their LinkedIn profile: 

  1. Author-# 1
  2. Author-# 2
  3. Author- #3

What it does?

  • SAP S/4HANA Posting: Generates reviewed PO line matches as INVOIC02 XML for SAP MM/FI processing.
  • SAP Concur Allocation: Exports AI match recommendations as JSON for AP review and invoice allocation.
  • Shared Matching Core: Same semantic scoring, ranking, and triage logic supports both S/4HANA and Concur modes.

Known Limitations (Phase 1)

  • Ranker weights are hand-tuned, not learned from data
  • No learning from user accept/reject feedback
  • English-centric descriptions
  • No batch matching endpoint
  • Client-side persistence only (no database / audit log)
  • SAP posting is not live IDoc download + manual “mark as uploaded” only
  • Binary Excel PO files (.xlsx/.xls) are not parsed; use CSV/JSON export
  • BOX → EA uses a fixed PoC pack size of 10 (not material-master driven)
  • Review UI has no free-form notes, escalate button, or arbitrary manual PO picker
  • Advanced UX components (search/filter, batch select, skeletons) exist in the component library but are not fully wired into the active workspace yet

Reference and Credits:

  • Machine Learning Course - by Stanford, by Professor Andrew Ng
  • AI Fundamentals Course (COMPSCI 713) - by University of Auckland, by Professors Thomas and Xinyu

  • Levenshtein Distance: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/1822502
  • Cosine Similarity: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/cosine-similarity
  • Ollama Sentence-BERT: https://ollama.com/library/all-minilm:l6-v2
  • Peppol documentation: https://docs.peppol.eu/poacc/upgrade-3/profiles/63-invoiceresponse/

entry.title: Designing Tiered Budget Controls Using Budget Address and AVC Derivation in SAP Funds Management
entry.content:
Introduction

When considering how best to manage budgets, public sector organizations must balance administrative overhead with the value delivered by budget controls. Any controls implemented carry the risk of generating additional overhead in the form of approvals, manual intervention, report reconciliation, change management, and more. Public sector leaders with deep industry experience are exceptionally well positioned to optimize their budgeting controls in the ways that matter most. This drives the first fundamental question that needs to be answered: What needs to be controlled?

For organizations using, or considering, SAP to manage their finances, it comes as no surprise that SAP offers lots of flexibility out of the box when it comes to budget controls. Budgeting and controls are managed directly within the SAP Funds Management (FM) module, however the inputs feeding the budget consumption often come from other parts of SAP such as procurement postings, travel and expense management, project systems, and flexible real estate to name a few.

Funds Management Account Assignment Derivation

SAP Funds Management Account Assignment (FMAA) is used to tag your system transactions, which can represent future commitments or actuals that consume the budgets maintained through the FM module. The account assignments are configurable within the standard system functionality and offer a high degree of flexibility to accommodate your organization's business requirements.

Within public cloud account assignment is driven by Substitution and Validation Rules within Fiori. For more information on the specifics, you can refer to SAP's course Implementing SAP S/4HANA Cloud for Public Sector IPSC1_EN_Col02 or reference the following high quality blog post authored by Atif Farooq: Budget Management in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud - SAP Community

On-premise or private cloud SAP offerings allow you to configure derivation rules, including the following step types:

These step types can be used in combination to trigger the appropriate account assignment scenarios. Ultimately, the account assignment derived for a transaction determines its posting address, which is linked to a budget address.

Funds Management Budget Address derivation can give you additional flexibility in how to direct these transactions to specific budgets, while Funds Management Availability Control (AVC) allows you to configure how the budget reacts to the transaction in case of upcoming or realized overages.

Budget Address Derivation

While mapping out your budget management strategy fewer things are as fundamental as your budget address derivation. Each time a budget-relevant transaction occurs it must find its way to the appropriate budget address. This address is where budget is loaded, monitored, adjusted, and controlled. 

The image below illustrates a budget address roll up based on configured derivation logic. 

With Budget Address Derivation you can define many‑to‑one (n:1) relationships that consolidate multiple posting addresses into a single budget address. This allows actuals and commitments to be recorded using detailed account assignments, while the available budget is centrally controlled at the aggregated budget address level across those postings. Leveraging budget address derivation allows you to create and manage budgets at a higher level while supporting detailed operational postings.

To configure budget address derivation, navigate through the following path using transaction SPRO for IMG configuration.

A simple example below shows 1 derivation rule used to roll up commitment items from both a range (items 0001 to 0002) and a specific value (0004) to commitment item 0001. This allows you to manage transactions tied to commitment items 0001, 0002, and 0004 all within the budget for 0001. In practice, the derivation strategy would be set up to reflect a real-world level of sophistication, but I have kept it as simple as possible for demonstration purposes within the blog. 

 

Leveraging budget address derivation allows you to structure budget management thoughtfully by grouping / rolling up addresses together within flat budget structures or multi-level budget structures, depending on your organization's requirements. 

Note: If you do not define an account assignment derivation, a standard 1:1 assignment is supported. This means that every FM account assignment you use as a posting address is assigned as a budget address itself.

Availability Control

Assigning budgets in SAP FM is the first step in controlling your organization's spending (expenses) and collections (revenue). Combining budget address derivation with availability control (AVC) object derivation can provide organizations with nested levels of control, supported by warnings or hard blocks as required. To illustrate this concept, the following simple example has been configured in a test system.

Navigating to the SPRO backend IMG configuration, you can find the Derivation Strategy for Control Objects through the following menu path. 

Note: If no AVC control object strategy is defined the system uses the budget address itself as the control object.

Important: After adjusting your AVC configuration in SPRO you may need to re-initialize the AVC object table through transaction FMAVCREINIT.

After completing the configuration outlined above the system is now triggering two powerful mechanisms to enable budget control:

  1. Budget address derivation 
    • After a posting address is either entered manually or derived, the system determines where the budget is held (i.e., the budget address in the budget structure) through budget address derivation. 
    • Converts posting addresses → budget address (n:1 possible).
  2. AVC object derivation
    • Once the budget address is determined, the system determines where availability control is checked by deriving the control objects.
    • Control objects can aggregate several budget addresses aligned to your organization's requirements.

How it all works together: Sequence in processing

In the example below, we can see that budget addresses are rolling up posting addresses across multiple commitment items, while the AVC object is rolling up multiple budget addresses across fund centers for a total aggregate consumable amount of 5,010,000.00. This aggregate budget amount can be managed with availability controls to trigger warnings or blockers at pre-defined thresholds as per your organization's requirements. 

The example above was created to help illustrate SAP FM's ability to leverage nested derivation for tiered control over budgets. 

Conclusion

A well-planned approach, based on both deep industry expertise and a strong understanding of standard SAP FM capabilities, can give business leaders the controls they need to drive operational excellence. Whether you are starting from scratch or optimizing an existing budget management model following a proven method can help you ensure you make the most of your investment. The high-level steps below outline general best practices to work towards an optimized budget control model:

  1. Define control objectives by tier: Identify where control is needed (posting, budget address, AVC level) and align each to business risk and oversight requirements

  2. Design FMAA derivation for clean posting inputs: Configure account assignment derivation to ensure all feeder transactions consistently produce accurate and usable posting addresses

  3. Configure budget address derivation for aggregation: Establish n:1 mappings to centralize budget management at the right level (e.g., program, fund center hierarchy) while preserving detailed postings

  4. Layer AVC object derivation for control strategy: Define AVC control objects to enforce budget checks at the appropriate aggregation level, independent of where the budget is stored

  5. Test, calibrate, and iterate controls: Validate end-to-end behavior (posting → budget → AVC), monitor false positives or gaps, and refine derivation and thresholds to balance control and usability

 

Ben Kane

entry.title: Introducing Functional Payment Approval in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud
entry.content:
Introduction and Business Value

Releasing outgoing payments is one of the most risk-sensitive activities in any finance department. A single erroneous or fraudulent transfer can result in significant financial loss yet traditional approval processes provide little systematic control over which payments are reviewed, by whom, and based on what criteria.

The functional payment approval process in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition addresses this directly. It enables flexible approval workflows for payments based on individual business criteria such as payment source, payment purpose, or payment risk signals. The result is that routine payments are released without unnecessary manual steps, while approval effort is concentrated where the risk actually lies tightening fraud control and reducing approver workload at the same time.

How It Works

Integrated into Your Payment Processes

Payment approval flows are integrated directly into your Accounts Payable and Accounts Receivable processes. They cover payments initiated through the ‘Manage Automatic Payments’ app (Fiori ID: F0770) and 'Automatic Payment Transactions for Payment Requests' app (Fiori ID: F111), including supplier payments, bank transfers and free-form payments. Payments can be flexibly grouped into logical functional approval sets, assigned a risk classification, and routed to the right approvers through SAP workflow.

Flexible, Attribute-Driven Strategies

Attribute-driven approval strategies let you configure which approval process, and which approvers apply based on the attributes of individual payments including payment purpose, debit/credit indicator, and payment origin. This removes previous restrictions on individual bank account configurations, making it practical to tailor the approval process at the level of granularity that real-world payment complexity demands. Direct debit payments, for example, can be processed fully automatically, eliminating unnecessary manual steps for pre-authorized, low-risk transaction types.

Risk-Based Intelligence

In addition, approval setups can incorporate key risk signals to determine the appropriate approval path. Risk signals can include whether a payment was entered free-form (vs. system-generated), whether it is routed to a one-time account, and whether the payment account data deviates from supplier master records. Low-risk payments are routed straight through; high-risk ones receive the scrutiny they warrant increasing straight-through processing rates and strengthening fraud controls at the same time.

Example of a Payment Approval Flow

Functional Payment ApprovalThis example illustrates how functional approval enables different payment workflows based on business scenarios and risk levels. Payments from various sources such as Accounts Payable (one-time vendor), Accounts Receivable (direct debit), HR-Payroll (salary/bonus), and Treasury Management (intra-company payment) are first classified through the ‘Manage Payment Business Rules’ app (Fiori ID: F9155) using the functional approval classifier.

Based on the risk assessment, each payment type follows a tailored approval path:

  • High risk payments require, for example, multi-level approval through multiple approvers
  • Medium risk payments require a single approver
  • Low risk payments are for example, auto approved

Once approved, payments proceed to their designated bank accounts for processing. The workflow demonstrates how you can assign simple or complex approval chains with different approvers based on your specific business requirements and risk tolerance. 

 

Key benefits at a glance:

  • Stronger payment security: Risk signals derived from payment source, one-time accounts, and master data deviations ensure that high-risk payments are never quietly released.
  • Higher straight-through processing: Routine, low-risk payments are released without manual review that reduces bottlenecks without reducing control.
  • Audit-proof compliance: Multi-level and parallel approvals, combined with team-based responsibilities, support four-eyes (and six-eyes) principles and segregation of duties. Every payment release is documented and traceable.
  • Approval processes that fit your payment policy: Approval strategies can be tailored by payment purpose, origin, and type, without restrictions tied to individual bank accounts so workflows mirror your internal payment policy instead of forcing workarounds.
  • Efficiency for approvers: All pending approvals surface in a single inbox with full context, including total amount, maximum risk, payee list, and approval progress. Batch-based approval sets additionally consolidation- related payments into a single approval task keeping approver workload low even at high payment volumes.

Want to know more?

Check out Part 2: Functional Payment Approval in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Configuration and FAQ  to learn more about activation steps, business rule configuration, and workflow setup!

For general information about the product, see Basic Payment Management.

entry.title: Functional Payment Approval in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Configuration and FAQ (Part 2)
entry.content:
Part 1 introduced functional payment approval and its risk-based approval capabilities. This blog walks through the configuration steps to activate and set up the feature.

1.    Getting Started: Activation and Prerequisites

Activating Functional Payment Approval in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud involves two main steps, which are enabling the feature toggle and defining functional approval classifiers. Both steps are performed through the ‘Manage Your Solution’ app. Before activating Functional Payment Approval, ensure that scope items 7MJ (Basic Payment Management) and J78 (Advanced Cash Operations) are included in your system configuration. Functional Payment Approval is integrated into your payment processes. The approval workflows are integrated into the payment runs initiated through

  • Manage Automatic Payments (Fiori ID: F0770)
  • Automatic Payment Transactions for Payment Request (Fiori ID: F111)

Step 1: Activate the Feature Toggle

Activate the feature toggle by navigating to: Manage Your Solution → Configure Your Solution → SSC-UI 106573 ‘Activate Business Features’ → Set PF2_PAYM_FOUND_FUNC_APPROVAL_2 to ‘Active’ and save.

Step 2: Define Functional Approval Classifiers (SSCUI 107268)

A functional approval classifier is the central categorization element of the payment approval process. It defines how payments are grouped into functional approval sets, which are the units that flow through the approval workflow. Each classifier carries a name, a description, and exactly one functional approval strategy.

The functional approval strategy assigned to a classifier controls how approval sets are created and processed.

Approval Strategy

System Behavior

Typical Use

Automatic Approval

Payments are released without creating a manual approval task

Low-risk, pre-authorized payment types (for example, direct debits)

Batch-Based Approval

All matching payments in a payment run are grouped into a single approval set

Payment types where a collective review is appropriate

Individual Approval

Each payment creates its own approval set

High-risk payments requiring individual scrutiny

The choice of strategy has direct operational consequences: A ‘batch-based’ approval keeps approver workload low by consolidating payments into one task, while payment with ‘individual approval’ strategy ensure in-depth reviews by creating single workflow instances per payment.

An approval classifier configuration could look as follows:

[Functional Approval Classifier Configuration in Manage Payment Business Rules App]

Step 3: Configure Business Rules

Functional payment approval relies on business rules that classify payments and determine how they are routed. The 'Manage Payment Business Rules' app allows you to derive individual business attributes based on complex rules that you configure. You can configure two types of components, which are payment risk classifier and functional approval classifier.

Payment Risk Classifier - You can set up payment risk classifiers to assess and categorize payments based on risk criteria. In the ‘Manage Payment Business Rules’ app, you set a risk score. The score determines the risk classification assigned to the payment. When creating a rule with payment risk classifier, you define the corresponding risk score. The system integrates key risk signals to assess each payment.

For example, you could create risk-related rules based on

  • Payment source tagging allowing distinction of free-form payments,
  • One-time accounts,
  • Deviating payment account data compared to master data records, or
  • Payee country.

Configuration settings could look like this:

[Payment Risk Calculation – Example]

All applicable rules will be evaluated and added to the overall sum of risks. The sum determines the risk classifier according to the following thresholds:

Risk Classifier

Risk Score Range

Low (L)

<15

Medium (M)

<30

High (H)

<60

Very High (V)

<100

For example, you might want to consider the payment risk classifier when determining the functional approval classifier.

Functional Approval Classifier - You can create and manage functional approval classifiers that determine approval requirements for payments based on specific criteria. The functional approval classifier acts as a criterion to control your approval flow during functional approval processing. In addition, it serves also as a grouping criterion to group payments into a dedicated approval group. You can define conditions within the classifier to specify when certain approval workflows should apply. For example, you can create rules based on payment type such as salary, or other payment attributes to route payments through appropriate approval processes.

[Functional Approval Classifier Rule Configuration]

Step 4: Setting Up Workflows and Approval Teams

After defining your business rules, you can create approval workflows that route payments to the appropriate approvers and set up the teams who will perform these approvals.

-       Manage Workflows for Payment Processing

Create approval workflows in the Manage Workflows for Payment Processing app. In the workflow configuration, you can flexibly set start conditions. For example, you could configure different workflows based on functional approval classifier and the paying company code. This way, depending on risk or other requirements, it is possible to apply stricter approval processes while assigning different approvers from various areas.

[Example of a Workflow Configuration]

As a newly introduced feature on the workflow, approvers can be assigned either by role or by team. In case of team assignment, it is possible to configure multiple approvers in parallel using the option ‘Two/Three recipients’.

[Workflow Step Configuration - Recipients and Approval Settings]

-       Manage Teams and Responsibilities

Ensure that approvers are added as team members by navigating to the Manage Teams and Responsibilities app. Select an existing team under type ‘Payment Approval’ and category ‘Payment Factory’ or create a new team by providing a global ID, adding team owners and team members with the function set to ‘Payment Monitoring’.

Enabling Email Notifications for Approvers

Approvers can receive email notifications when payments are pending their approval. This section covers how to configure email templates and enable notifications in your approval workflows.

Prerequisites

Before enabling email notifications, ensure that approvers are added as team members.

Configuring Email Templates

  • Customize the email notification template by navigating to the Maintain Email Templates app → Search for the pre-delivered template PF2_PAYFN_NOTIFY_APPROVED/ PF2_PAYFN_TIMEOUT_APPROVAL → Copy → Enter a new template ID → Modify template details and select language → Create.

Enabling Email Notifications in Workflows

Before enabling email notifications, the following templates must be copied in the Maintain Email Templates app:

  • PF2_PAYFN_NOTIFY_APPROVER
  • PF2_PAYFN_TIMEOUT_APPROVAL

Once the templates are copied, it is possible to include notifications in the workflow.

To enable email notifications in the workflow steps, configure the 'Deadlines' section by creating a deadline, selecting the Send Mail Notification action, and selecting the team whose recipients should be notified. Save and activate the workflow for notifications to be sent. 

[Setting up Email Notification in Workflow]

Note that invalid email addresses can prevent notifications from being sent entirely. For example, prohibited domains or incorrectly formatted email addresses will cause notification failures. For troubleshooting email notification issues, refer to: https://me.sap.com/notes/2838665.

Enable Decision Reasons for Approvals

It is possible to activate dedicated decision reasons within the payment approval process. To enable this, access your configuration environment via SSCUI ‘Edit Decision Reasons’ (SSCUI ID 104740) and configure corresponding decision texts for your approval workflows.

FAQs

1. Does a payment run always create a single approval group?

There is now more flexibility regarding grouping. It is possible to create multiple approval groups for a single payment run, resulting in several payment batches being sent to the bank. Each batch may contain fewer payments depending on the approval requirements.

2. Can I approve payments from multiple payment methods and house bank accounts together in Functional Payment Approval? How are these payment batches sent to the bank?

Yes, it is possible to approve multiple payment methods and generate only a single file, if this is configured in the automatic payment configuration and if the payment medium format is the same for multiple payment methods. A single payment batch will be created, automatically approved, and routed as a single file to SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity.

3. What happens to payments that are currently approved using 'Approve Bank Payments' when Functional Payment Approval is active?

When payments are routed through the Functional Payment Approval process (including automatically approved payments), they will not be sent to 'Approve Bank Payments'. Instead, the 'Approve Bank Payments' approval step is skipped entirely.

4. I cannot see the feature toggle in my system. What should I do?

Ensure that scope item 7MJ (Basic Payment Management) is activated in your system configuration.

5. How do I configure amount-based rules for credit transfers?

When configuring amount-based rules for credit transfers, the amount must be set to less than 0 as the balance on the paying bank account will be reduced by this amount.

6. Why are both business rules and workflows required? What should be configured in business rules versus workflow settings?

Business rules for functional approval classifiers are relevant to decide if the functionality is active and to assign also ‘Automatic Approvals’ without additional workflow to corresponding payments. Moreover, the approval classifier derived in the business rules supports the separation of payments into distinct approval groups. Once the payments are sent to the workflow the grouping remains in place.

Regarding configuration, complex rule conditions that require more frequent changes are typically configured in the business rules for the approval classifier, whereas the workflow is typically more static for the approval process and team configuration.

To learn more about the feature overview and business value, see Part 1 - Introducing Functional Payment Approval in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud. For more information, see Basic Payment Management.

entry.title: How CCS Works in Actual Costing (S/4HANA Public Cloud Edition)
entry.content:
Cost Component Split (CCS) is one of the most powerful features in SAP Actual Costing and also the one that generates the most questions.

After running CKMLCP, you may wonder: where exactly do those numbers in the Periodic Unit Price (PUP) breakdown come from? why does one component show a negative value in order settlement? And why is there variable cost on a component in the actual result?

This blog walks through the full CCS lifecycle using a concrete example, from configuration to CKMLCP settlement, so you can trace every value back to its origin.

  • Master Data: Material Standard Cost Estimates and Activity Type
  • Configuration: Define Cost Component Structure (SSCUI 102427)
  • Goods Movements and Order Settlement
  • CKMLCP: Allocating Actual CCS to Consumption and Inventory

Master Data: Material Standard Cost Estimates and Activity Type

Raw Material RM124

RM124 is an externally procured material. Its standard cost is 0.35 EUR/PC (35.00 EUR/100 PC lot) and entirely falls into component 101 Direct Material (100% variable). This is the CCS template that will be applied when RM124 is received from a purchase order.

Standard Cost Estimate of RM124

Semi-Finished Material SG124_MA06

SG124_MA06 is a manufactured material with standard price 0.89 EUR/PC (88.51 EUR/100 PC lot). Its BOM and routing drive a richer CCS as below:

Standard Cost Estimate of SG124_MA06

The costing structure shows:

  • RM124 (100 PC × 0.35 = 35.00) maps to 101 Direct Material via cost element 51100000.
  • Activity types 3, 1, 11 at cost center 10101301 map to 203 Set-Up Time, 202 Machine, and 201 Personnel Time respectively.
  • Material overhead (cost element 94111000) and Production overhead (94112000) map to 109 Material Overhead and 209 Production Overhead respectively.

Itemization of SG124_MA06 Standard Cost

 In the Itemization view of SG124_MA06, the cost elements are derived by the system. For example:

  • For a BOM component like RM124, CK11N (Create Material Cost Estimate) simulates the goods issue using account of GBB/VBR (consumption account for production, which is associated with the respective movement type 261):
    • Automatic Account Determination (SSCUI 100297) resolves GBB/VBR + RM124's valuation class to G/L account 51100000.
    • Define Cost Component Structure (SSCUI 102427) then maps 51100000 to cost component 101 Direct Material. See Configuration section.
  • For activity types, the cost element (e.g. 94311000 for activity type 11) is defined directly on the activity type master data and does not go through account determination SSCUI. See below for more info.

Activity Type Master Data

Taking activity type 11 (Personnel Hours) as an example, in its master data (app Manage Activity Types), allocation cost element 94311000 is specified for transferring cost of labor from a cost center to a production order when confirming personnel hours, e.g. in CO11N (Confirm Production Order Operation).

Master Data of Activity Type 11

Btw, the Actual Price Indicator = 5 means the activity type uses an actual cost rate determined at period end. During the period, confirmations post at the planned rate; at period end, CKMLCP revalues them using the actual rate, generating a price difference that rolls up into the manufactured material's CCS.

Configuration: Define Cost Component Structure (SSCUI 102427)

Define Cost Component Structure (SSCUI 102427, also known as OKTZ) is where you set up cost components and map cost elements (G/L accounts) to them. The same structure is used for both standard cost estimates and Actual Costing.

The structure Y1 used in our example defines the following components:

Cost Component Structure Y1

Cost Element to Component Mapping

Each cost component maps to one or more cost element intervals. As you can see:

101 Component: Direct Material

  • Cost elements 51100000 ~ 54400000 covering material consumption postings are all mapped to component 101 (Direct Material). This includes cost element 51100000 used when issuing RM124 to a production order discussed earlier.
  • The allocation cost element 94311000 of activity type 11 (Personnel Hours) is mapped to component 201 (Personnel Time).

201 Component: Personnel Time

Important Component Attributes

Note the following 2 important attributes of a component:

  • "Inventory Valuation Relevant": When set to Relevant, the component's value contributes to inventory valuation and is included in the PUP calculation. When set to Not Relevant (e.g. Sales and Administration Costs), the component is shown in cost reports but does not affect the revaluation in Actual Costing.
  • "Roll up Cost Component": It means costs roll up to the next higher costing level, e.g. from personnel costs to the manufactured material's CCS.

Component Attributes

Goods Movements and Order Settlement

Every goods movement, e.g. a purchase order GR, a GI to a production order, a GR from a production order, writes a row to the CCS table (MLDOCCCS), using the standard price proportions from the cost component structure as the template.

Purchase of RM124

In period 7/2026, 100 PC of RM124 were received against purchase order 4500000060/10. The goods receipt (GR) is posted with price diff. (-22.25 EUR) and exchange rate diff. (+1.54 EUR) in addition to the preliminary cost valued at standard price of 0.35 EUR/PC, as seen in Material Price Analysis (CKM3N) :

Purchase of RM124

At the time of the GR (and invoice receipt, if applicable), MLDOCCCS is written at 100% Direct Material (component 101) with the following:

  • Preliminary value split = 35.00 EUR for 100 PC.
  • Price difference of -22.25 EUR (price lower than standard)
  • Exchange rate difference of +1.54 EUR

Production Order Settlement

When the order is completed and settled, as shown in app Order Cost Details - Event-Based, order 1000922 accumulates actual costs across three debit transaction types:

Cost Details of Production Order 1000922

  • Confirmations (Activities)

The three confirmation lines correspond to activity types 1 (Machine), 3 (Set-Up), and 11 (Personnel Hours) at cost center 10101301. As shown previously, cost element 94311000 (the allocation cost element of activity type 11) maps to component 201 (Personnel Time) via SSCUI 102427.

  • Goods Issues (Component Consumption)

40 PC of RM124 were issued to the production order at the standard price of 0.35 EUR/PC = 14.00 EUR. Cost element 51100000 maps to 101 Direct Material. At the time of the GI, MLDOCCCS for RM124 is updated with a consumption row at 100% Direct Material.

  • Overhead Absorption

Overhead keys absorb indirect costs onto the order. Cost element 94111000 maps to Material Overhead (109); 94112000 maps to Production Overhead (209).

The Goods Receipt credits the order at standard price when finished goods are received into stock, reducing the order balance:

  • Goods Receipt (Production Output)

50 PC of SG124_MA06 are received into stock. The GR credits the production order at standard price 0.89 EUR/PC = 44.50 EUR (account 55100000, determined by transaction key GBB/AUF of movement type 101).

At the time of the GR, MLDOCCCS for SG124_MA06 is written using the standard cost proportions from the CK13N estimate (88.51 EUR/100 PC): each component's share of 88.51 EUR is scaled to the 44.50 EUR GR value, e.g. 101 Direct Material = 35.00/88.51 × 44.50 = 17.59 EUR. The full split:

  • 101 Direct Material: 17.59 EUR,
  • 109 Material Overhead: 1.23 EUR,
  • 201 Personnel: 9.24 EUR,
  • 202 Machine: 2.08 EUR,
  • 203 Set-Up: 12.02 EUR,
  • 209 Prod Overhead: 2.34 EUR

total 44.50 EUR. See below CKM3N screen for the GR value CCS:

Goods Receipt of SG124_MA06

  • Order settlement: Debits (34.40 + 14.00 + 4.42 = 52.82) minus GR credit 44.50 = +8.32 EUR remaining on the order. This is the variance on production order 1000922 (8.32 EUR) settles to SG124_MA06, creating a price difference visible in CKM3N.

How the Order Settlement CCS Is Calculated

The 8.32 EUR remaining balance on order 1000922 settles to SG124_MA06. The CCS split of this settlement amount is simply the difference between actual debits and GR credit, calculated component by component.

Each debit posted to the order carries a cost element, which is mapped to a CCS component:

  • GI of RM124 (51100000): 14.00 EUR → component 101 Direct Material
  • Activity type 1 Machine (94301000): 4.13 EUR → component 202 Machine Time
  • Activity type 3 Set-Up (94303000): 11.95 EUR → component 203 Set-Up Time
  • Activity type 11 Personnel (94311000): 18.32 EUR → component 201 Personnel Time
  • Overhead Material (94111000): 0.98 EUR → component 109 Material Overhead
  • Overhead Production (94112000): 3.44 EUR → component 209 Production Overhead

The GR of 50 PC at standard price 0.89 EUR/PC = 44.50 EUR credits the order using the standard CCS proportions of SG124_MA06 from CK13N (101: 17.59 EUR; 109: 1.23 EUR; 201: 9.24 EUR; 202: 2.08 EUR; 203: 12.02 EUR; 209: 2.34 EUR).

Order Settlement

The settlement CCS is then debits minus GR credit per component:

This matches the CCS columns I highlighted in the blue box on CKM3N screen. The negative values on, e.g. 101 Direct Material (-3.59 EUR), are not errors. The settlement CCS is calculated as actual debits minus GR credit, component by component. For Direct Material, the GR already credited 17.59 EUR at standard, but only 14.00 EUR of actual input cost was posted so the settlement value is negative, meaning the standard GR overstated this component.

CKMLCP: Allocating Actual CCS to Consumption and Inventory

After posting all period transactions, CKMLCP actual costing run is executed. For SG124_MA06, this involves the following:

1. Actual cost differences from lower BOM/routing levels (input materials and activities) roll up into SG124_MA06's actual value. Taking activity 11 as an example:

Activity After CKMLCP Settlement

 The actual rate (36.73 EUR/H) is lower than the standard (55.01 EUR/H). CKMLCP revalues all activity confirmations on production orders from standard to actual.

For order 1000922, the confirmation of 0.333 H at standard is 18.32 EUR (≈ 55.01 × 0.333). In addition, the revaluation price difference of -6.09 EUR is determined (≈ (36.73-55.01) × 0.333) and rolled up as a price difference into SG124_MA06, as seen from the CKM3N screen below:

SG124_MA06 After CKMLCP Settlement

Similarly, all other consumed activities (-9.28 EUR of ATY 3, 8.11 EUR of ATY 1) and BOM materials (-8.28 EUR of RM124) have their price differences rolled up to the finished product SG124_MA04. Meanwhile, CCS splits are also carried over.

2. All received differences and actual values together form the Cumulative Inventory row (60 PC, actual value 47.18 EUR, PUP 0.79 EUR/PC). The per-component actual CCS at the cumulative level sums to:

  • 101 Direct Material 15.72 EUR,
  • 109 Material Overhead 0.98 EUR,
  • 201 Personnel 12.23 EUR,
  • 202 Machine 12.24 EUR,
  • 203 Set-Up 2.57 EUR,
  • 209 Production Overhead 3.44 EUR.

3. Cumulative actual value is allocated to consumption and ending inventory in proportion to quantity. With 10 PC consumed and 50 PC in ending inventory out of 60 PC cumulative:

  • Consumption (10/60 = 1/6): 47.18 × 1/6 = 7.86 EUR
  • Ending Inventory (50/60 = 5/6): 47.18 × 5/6 = 39.32 EUR

4. The same ratios, i.e. 1/6 and 5/6 apply component by component, e.g. 101 Direct Material:

  • Consumption: 15.72 × 1/6 = 2.62 EUR
  • Ending inventory: 15.72 × 5/6 = 13.10 EUR

Two Consistency Rules

The calculations above illustrate two consistency rules the system enforces across every row and column in CKM3N:

  • Row rule: for every row, the sum of all cost component values equals the Actual Value. For example, the Cumulative Inventory row: 15.72 + 0.98 + 12.23 + 12.24 + 2.57 + 3.44 = 47.18 EUR.
  • Column rule: for every column, e.g. Actual Value and each CCS component, Beginning Inventory + Receipts = Cumulative Inventory = Consumption + Ending Inventory. For example, component 101 Direct Material: 0 + 15.72 = 15.72 = 2.62 + 13.10.

Why does a component show a small variable amount in the actual CCS when the standard cost estimate had zero variable planned?

When you compare the standard cost estimate (CK13N) with the actual PUP cost component split after CKMLCP, you may occasionally notice a small variable amount, e.g. -0.01 or +0.01 on a component that is configured as 100% fixed in standard cost estimate. This is a rounding artifact, not an error.

To understand why, consider how CKMLCP distributes cumulative inventory values to consumption and ending inventory. It calculates the total value and the fixed value of each cost component using two different quantity-proportion methods:

  • Cumulative method: The total value is calculated cumulatively across all rows (2-dimensional algorithm). The system accumulates a running total and scales it once, ensuring the column sum is always exact.
  • Row-by-row method: The fixed value is calculated row by row, i.e. each row is scaled independently (1-dimensional algorithm).
Example:

Cumulative inventory: 11 KG. For simplification, actual value 18.00 EUR is composed of only two 100%-fixed cost components:

  • Raw materials (RM) = 9.00 EUR,
  • Machine hours (MH) = 9.00 EUR.

  • Row 2 (cumulative 8/11):

    • The row-by-row method scales MH alone (9 EUR) by 8/11, getting 2.46. The missing cent is the phantom variable: −0.01.

  • Row 3 (cumulative 11/11): the remainder absorbs the difference. Total: 18.00 − 13.09 − 2.45 = 2.46. Fixed: 9.00 − 6.55 = 2.45. Variable = +0.01. 

Both methods use the same quantity proportion but apply it at different points. Since variable is derived as total minus fixed, this one-cent difference shows up as a small non-zero variable, even though no variable cost was planned for that component.

Note: These ±0.01 amounts have no impact on FI postings, the PUP, or your inventory balance.

Actual Price (PUP) CCS Result for SG124_MA06 After CKMLCP

After CKMLCP settlement, SG124_MA06's actual PUP = 0.79 EUR/PC is determined (= cumulative actual value 47.18 EUR /cumulative quantity 60 PC).

The PUP CCS (visible in the Cost Components for Price view of CKM3N with Type of Price: Periodic Unit Price, base quantity 100 PC) is derived the same way: each component's cumulative actual CCS value is divided by cumulative quantity and scaled to the costing lot size of 100 PC.

For example, 101 Direct Material: 15.72 EUR (60 PC) ÷ 60 × 100 = 26.32 EUR per 100 PC. The full result per 100 PC:

  • 101 Direct Material 26.32 EUR,
  • 109 Mat. Overhead 1.64 EUR,

Compared with the standard price CCS below:

  • Direct Material (101) is lower than standard (26.32 vs 35.20): This is partially because raw material RM124's actual price was lower than standard (PUP 0.14 vs std 0.35), and this flows into SG124_MA06 via multilevel price determination.
  • Personnel Time (201) is higher than standard: This is due to more personnel hours were spent (actual 0.333 H vs planned 0.168 H) as seen from Production Order Settlement although actual cost rate (36.73 EUR/H) is lower than planned (55.01 EUR/H).

Summary: The CCS Lifecycle

Putting it all together, here is when each CCS value is written and what drives it:

Proportional to quantity ratio

Conclusion

CCS in SAP S/4HANA Actual Costing is not a black box, every value has a clear origin in either the cost component structure configuration, the standard cost estimate, or the actual costs posted through goods movements and production activities. Understanding these origins enables us to explain why a particular component value differs between standard and actual, and which business event drove the change.
