entry.title: Ask Me Anything with SAP Champions – Monthly Series (Session 6 Responses)
entry.content:
Hello, beloved SAP Community!

As part of the Ask Me Anything with SAP Champions blog post, I received several interesting questions around SAP FICO, international rollouts, career development, and automation through various channels.

I have consolidated the questions and done my best to address them here, grouping them by topic to make the discussion easier to navigate.

So, let’s get started! For each topic, you will first find the original question, followed by my answer and perspective.

A quick note on context: the answers reflect my personal perspective as an SAP Champion, with a focus on SAP FICO and international rollouts. They are based on my knowledge and experience at this point in time. As we all know, SAP is constantly evolving, and there is rarely a one-size-fits-all answer—especially when it comes to automation and Finance processes.

I therefore always welcome an open and ongoing dialogue. Sharing different perspectives, experiences, and lessons learned is one of the things that makes the SAP Community so valuable.

I hope you find the answers useful—and perhaps they will spark some new questions, ideas, or discussions of your own.

Let’s dive in!

 

1. SAP Implementation & International Rollouts

Q: What is one of the most important lessons you have learned from real-life SAP implementations? 

Submitted by MRobalinho (SAP Champion)

A: There are many lessons I have learned over the years, but if I had to choose just one, I would say: Understand the business behind the SAP system. When you are working on an SAP implementation, it is very easy to become focused on configuration, transactions, requirements, and technical solutions.

But SAP is there to support the business. So before asking: How do we configure this? I think we should first ask: Why does the business need this? That understanding makes a huge difference when you have to make design decisions.

Another lesson I have learned is that communication is just as important as SAP knowledge. On global projects, you work with people from different countries, cultures, companies, and levels of SAP experience. Sometimes the biggest challenge is not finding the technical solution. It is getting everyone aligned around the solution.

So, for me, a good SAP professional needs to be three things: A functional expert, a problem solver, and a good communicator. You can have excellent SAP knowledge, but if you cannot explain the solution and get people aligned, the project will struggle.

 

Q: What are the three most critical aspects when migrating from ECC to newer SAP versions?

Submitted by eamarce23

A: There are three particularly important areas:

1. Understand your existing system before you start: Do not assume that everything in your current system needs to be copied. A move to SAP S/4HANA is an opportunity to review your custom developments, processes, interfaces, and configurations. Ask yourself the following questions: Do we still need this? Can we simplify it? Can we replace it with standard functionality?

Migration should not automatically mean carrying years of historical decisions into the new environment.

2. Focus on business processes and data—not only the technical migration: From an FICO perspective, you need to understand the impact on areas such as the Universal Journal, Asset Accounting, Controlling, user experience, and integrations with other systems. The objective should not simply be to get the system technically migrated. The real objective is to make sure that the business processes work correctly and that the organization can take advantage of the new capabilities.

3. Involve the business early and manage change carefully: Users need to understand not only what is changing, but also why it is changing. Testing, training, communication, and stakeholder involvement are therefore extremely important. And on global projects, I would add another important consideration: have a clear global template while still allowing for the local requirements that are genuinely necessary. 

So, for me, a successful move to S/4HANA is not just a technical project. It is a combination of technology, business processes, data, and people.

 

Q: What are three aspects that people often forget to take into account, but that are also critical?

Submitted by eamarce23

A: This is a great follow-up question because some of the most important factors are not always the ones that appear first on the project plan. If I had to choose three, I would say:

1. The people: It is easy to focus on processes, configuration, data, and technology and forget that people ultimately have to use the solution. A technically perfect solution can still fail if the users do not understand it, do not trust it, or were not sufficiently involved in designing and testing it.

2. The exceptions: Projects often focus on the “happy path”: what should happen when everything works as expected. But real businesses are full of exceptions.  What happens when a posting fails? What happens when data is missing? What happens when a local requirement does not fit the global template? These scenarios need to be considered before go-live, not discovered for the first time in production.

3. What happens after go-live: Go-live is not the end of the project. It is the beginning of the operational life of the solution. Support processes, ownership, monitoring, knowledge transfer, documentation, and continuous improvement should therefore be considered from the beginning. In my experience, thinking beyond go-live is one of the things that separates a successful implementation from a technically successful implementation.

 

Q: You've worked on many global rollouts. What would you say are the biggest challenges?

Submitted anonymously via Forms

A: One of the biggest challenges is finding the right balance between global standardization and local requirements. In a global rollout, you want to have a global template that can be reused across countries. At the same time, every country has its own legal, tax, accounting, and business requirements. The challenge is deciding what really needs to be different locally and what can be standardized.

Another major challenge is communication. You can have teams in different countries, different time zones, and with very different levels of SAP experience. Making sure everyone understands the global template, the decisions that have been made, and their responsibilities is extremely important.

And I would add change management. A global rollout is not just about configuring SAP. You are changing the way people work. If you do not involve the business and users early enough, even a technically excellent solution can have problems during go-live.

After many rollouts, I have learned that the technical solution is only one part of the project. People, communication, and business understanding are equally important.

 

2. Career Development & Working on Global Projects

Q: How many years of experience are essential for finding remote SAP jobs? I have two years of experience and can't find one yet.

Submitted anonymously via Forms

A: I don't think there is a specific number of years that makes someone ready for a remote job. Of course, experience helps, but I think the more important question is: What can you do independently? If you have two years of SAP experience, I would not tell you to wait another three or five years before looking for a remote opportunity. Instead, I would recommend becoming very strong in a specific SAP area, understanding the end-to-end business process, and being able to clearly explain what you have actually done on projects.

Remote work also requires strong communication skills. When you are not sitting next to your colleagues, you need to be able to explain problems clearly, document your work, manage your time, and communicate effectively with people from different countries and cultures.

I would also avoid limiting your search to positions called “SAP Consultant.” Look at implementation projects, support roles, internal SAP positions, and international opportunities where remote or hybrid work is possible.

And finally, networking is extremely important. In SAP, opportunities often come through people you have worked with or people you have met through the community. Your SAP network can sometimes be just as important as your profile.

So my advice would be: Don't focus only on the number of years you have worked. Focus on the value you can bring, the skills you can demonstrate, and the problems you can solve.

 

Q: How can we work on FI/CO global projects?

Submitted anonymously via Forms

A: First, you need to develop both strong functional knowledge and international project skills. For FICO, I would recommend understanding the processes end to end. Don't focus only on individual transactions or configuration steps. Understand how a business process works from beginning to end and how FICO interacts with other areas such as MM, SD, and PP.

Then, if you want to work on global projects, you need to understand that every country has its own requirements. You need to be comfortable working with local teams while also understanding the global template and the decisions made at the global level.

English is also extremely important. On a global project, you may be working with people from several countries, and being able to communicate clearly in English can make a huge difference.

My other recommendation would be to get involved in international projects as early as possible. Even if your first role isn't an SAP consultant position, try to participate in workshops, testing, data migration, or cutover activities. Those experiences will make your profile much stronger. 

And you don't need 10 or 15 years of experience to work on a global project. You need the right skills, the right attitude, and a willingness to work with people from different cultures and backgrounds.

 

Q: After 20 years, what would you say is the most important skill for an SAP consultant?

Submitted anonymously via Forms

A: I would say communication and the ability to understand the business. Of course, you need strong SAP knowledge. But after 20 years, I've seen that the consultants who are most successful aren't necessarily the people who know the most transactions or configuration options.

They are the people who can understand what the business is trying to achieve and translate that into an SAP solution. You also need to be able to communicate with different audiences. You might have to speak with a CFO in the morning, a business user in the afternoon, and a technical consultant later that day. You need to be able to explain the same issue in a way that makes sense to each person.

So, my advice would be: Don't become just an SAP expert. Become someone who can solve business problems using SAP.

 

Q: How can someone develop their career in the SAP ecosystem today?

Submitted anonymously via Forms

A: There are many more opportunities today than when I started, but I think the key is to avoid trying to learn everything at once. Choose an area and build a strong foundation. For example, if you're interested in Finance, learn FI/CO properly and, importantly, understand the business processes behind it. Then gradually expand your knowledge. Learn about S/4HANA, integration with other modules, data, analytics, automation, and now AI.

I would also strongly recommend getting practical experience as early as possible. Training and certifications are useful, but working on a real implementation, rollout, migration, support issue, or business process gives you a completely different level of understanding.

And finally, build your network. The SAP Community is a fantastic resource. Attend events, participate in discussions, follow SAP professionals, share what you're learning, and don't be afraid to ask questions. You never know where your next opportunity will come from.

 

3. Learning SAP FICO

Q: What about someone who is learning FICO? Would you recommend YouTube channels?

Submitted anonymously via Forms

A: Definitely. There is an enormous amount of free content available today, which is something that didn't exist when I started my career. There are several people and resources I would recommend. For example, Marssel Vilaca has some very useful SAP Finance content, particularly for people who are starting out. I would also recommend the How-to series on SAP Finance from SAP Press, because it provides practical information and is useful when you want to go deeper into specific topics. Vikram Fotani is another person worth following for SAP Finance content.

But I would give one important warning: Don't just watch videos passively. Try to reproduce what you're learning in a system, if you have access to one. Configure something. Test a process. Make a mistake. Then try to understand why it didn't work. For me, that's when the real learning happens.

 

Q: If you could give one piece of advice to someone starting their SAP career today, what would it be?

Submitted anonymously via Forms

A: I would say: Don't focus only on learning SAP; learn the business. If you're learning FI/CO, don't just memorize transaction codes or configuration steps. Understand why a company needs accounts payable, accounts receivable, asset accounting, controlling, financial closing, or management reporting. Then learn how those processes connect to each other and to other SAP modules. 

My second piece of advice would be to get hands-on experience as soon as possible. Even if you're starting with support or a small project, take every opportunity to understand how a real SAP system works. 

And finally, don't be afraid of changes in technology. Keep learning. Twenty years in SAP has taught me that the technology will change continuously, but people who are willing to learn and adapt will always have opportunities.

 

4. Looking at SAP Then and Now

Q: Looking back at your career, what has changed the most in SAP?

Submitted anonymously via Forms

A: Almost everything! But if I had to choose one thing, I would say the speed of change. When I started working with SAP, the focus was very much on traditional ERP systems, transactions, configuration, and on-premise implementations. Today, we're talking about SAP S/4HANA, Public Cloud, BTP, APIs, Analytics, automation, and AI. The role of the SAP consultant is also changing. You can't just know your module anymore. You need to understand integration, data, business processes, and increasingly technologies such as AI and automation.

Another big change is the amount of knowledge available. When I started, learning often meant books, classroom training, and learning from colleagues. Today, you have SAP Community, YouTube, blogs, podcasts, online courses, and many other resources. That's a huge advantage for people starting their careers today.

 

Q: What does the future look like for SAP FICO professionals?

Submitted anonymously via Forms

A: I think the future is actually very exciting. There will always be a need for people who understand Finance and business processes. What will change is the way we perform the work. AI and automation will increasingly take care of repetitive activities, data processing, reconciliations, reporting, and other tasks.

That doesn't mean SAP Finance professionals will become less important. I think it means their role will become more valuable in areas where business understanding, analysis, decision-making, and problem-solving are required. For someone working in FICO today, I would recommend keeping the strong Finance foundation but adding new skills: SAP S/4HANA, Public Cloud, BTP, Analytics, automation, integration, and AI.

And I think the biggest opportunity is for people who can connect all of these areas together. So I don't see AI as something SAP FICO professionals should be afraid of. I see it as a tool that can help us become more productive and spend more time solving meaningful business problems.

The future SAP Finance professional, in my opinion, won't just be someone who knows how to configure FICO. It will be someone who understands Finance, technology, data, and the business—and knows how to bring all four together.

 

5. SAP FICO in Practice: Automation Questions

Q: How would you automatically send dunning letters at different levels?

Submitted by Ankush Kumar via Forms

A: In SAP, you can configure the dunning procedure to define different dunning levels and the rules associated with each level. You can define things such as the number of days in arrears, grace periods, minimum amounts, and the content or form of the dunning notice.

The dunning run can then determine which customers and open items need to be included and assign the appropriate dunning level. From an automation perspective, you can schedule the dunning run as a background job. The system can automatically identify the relevant customers, calculate the appropriate dunning level, generate the correspondence, and, depending on the setup, send the dunning notices electronically.

The important point is that you don't necessarily need someone to manually run the process every time. You can design it as a scheduled and controlled process, with the appropriate approvals and monitoring around it.

 

Q: The bank sends two bank statement files every day. Someone currently downloads them manually and runs FF_5. Can this be automated?

Submitted by Ankush Kumar via Forms

A: Yes, absolutely. This is a classic opportunity for automation. Instead of having someone manually download the files every day and execute FF_5, you can automate the process of receiving the bank statement files and importing them into SAP.

The exact solution depends on the number of banks, the file format, and the SAP landscape. In an S/4HANA environment, you would typically look at the available multi-bank connectivity rather than simply thinking about the manual FF_5 process.

The key is to automate the entire chain: Receive the file → make it available to SAP → import it → process the statement → monitor the results. And I think it is important to look beyond simply automating FF_5. If you're designing the process today, look at the complete end-to-end solution and ask whether there are better standard SAP options available in the current system.

 

Q: So, automation needs monitoring as well?

Submitted by Ankush Kumar via Forms

A: Absolutely. Automation without monitoring can actually create bigger problems than a manual process. If a person downloads the bank statement every morning and something goes wrong, they will probably notice it. But if you automate the process and the file isn't received, the interface fails, or some transactions aren't posted correctly, you need a mechanism to detect that. 

So whenever I design an automated process, I always think about two things:  Automation and exception handling. What happens when everything works? That's the easy part. The more important question is: What happens when something doesn't work? You need monitoring, alerts, logs, and a clear responsibility for who investigates and resolves the exception.

 

Q: How would you automatically post recurring entries for a whole year?

Submitted by Ankush Kumar via Forms

A: For a traditional recurring entry process in SAP, you can create a recurring document with the relevant company code, accounts, amounts, dates, and frequency, and then execute the recurring entry run to generate the actual accounting documents according to the defined schedule. For example, if you have a monthly expense that is the same every month, you can create the recurring document and schedule the process rather than manually posting the same document twelve times.

However, in newer S/4HANA environments, I would also consider whether a recurring journal entry or another standard automation capability is more appropriate for the specific requirement. The important thing is to understand the business requirement first. For that, ask: 

  • Is the amount always the same?
  • Does the posting need to happen on a specific date?
  • Does it need to be approved?
  • Does it change from month to month?
  • What happens if the posting fails?

Once you understand the requirement, you can choose the most appropriate standard SAP functionality rather than simply automating a manual posting.

 

Final Thoughts

Looking through all these questions, I actually see one common thread connecting many of them. Whether we are talking about an international rollout, an S/4HANA migration, career development, or FICO automation, the same principles keep coming back:

  • Understand the business.
  • Understand the people.
  • Understand the process end to end.
  • Communicate clearly.
  • Use standard functionality where it makes sense.
  • And always think about what happens when things don't go according to plan.

Technology will continue to change. SAP will continue to evolve. New tools, platforms, and AI capabilities will change the way we work. But I believe the fundamentals will remain remarkably consistent. The ability to understand a business problem, work with people, design a sustainable solution, and continuously learn will always be valuable.

Thank you to everyone who submitted a question, whether through the blog post, Forms, or other channels. And please don't consider this conversation closed! What has been your experience with SAP FICO, international rollouts, automation, or career development? I would love to hear your perspectives, lessons learned, and perhaps even your answers to some of these questions.

See you in the comments!

Hello Community,

This blog is an outocme of my recent project experience wherein the Field ACDOCA-FIPEX is empty after migrating to S/4HANA. During brownfield conversions, this was observed and the analysis is as below.

Behavior - The field FIPEX will be empty for all the documents posted before S/4HANA OP2020 release. In case the migrated records were posted in ECC or other release lower than S/4HANA OP2020, FIPEX will be empty. This is not a bug but a desired result of the migration. 

Analysis - This is not a bug but a desired result of the migration. 

Next steps - If the field needs to be filled then the data migration team should take this up as a specific requirement and include the mapping of BSEG tables to ACDOCA. It is always to do an impact analysis before proceeding with next steps.

SAP Notes for reference - 2912327 

Thanks.

Shubham

entry.title: Before You Change a Settlement Rule: What the History Is Telling You
entry.content:
The Situation

Project controllers and system administrators need to change settlement rules from time to time. A project moves to a different department. A cost center is reorganized. An investment project was initially tied to the wrong asset. The reason varies, but the question is always the same: can I just update the rule and run settlement again? And the answer - it depends. A rule already used cannot be changed, other rules can.

Before changing a settlement rule that’s already been used, read your settlement history by period and ledger to understand in which context the rule was used. Then decide if you want to correct the past (reverse and re‑settle) or govern the future (change rules going forward only).

This differentiation is important because settlement rules define where your actuals flow. If a rule has already produced postings, changing it would lead to inconsistencies within one financial period.

This post explains how settlement history works in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud and Private Cloud with Universal Parallel Accounting (UPA) active, what to look for before making any changes, and how to correctly sequence a rule change.

 

Why Validity Periods Exist on Distribution Rules

A cost object (e.g. WBS element) typically has a lifecycle that spans multiple fiscal periods, sometimes years. The business reality of where costs should go often changes during that lifecycle. Validity periods let you define different rules for different time windows, and the system automatically applies the correct rule based on the posting period of the settlement run.

Without time-based rules, you would either:

  • apply one static rule for the entire life of the cost object (inflexible and often incorrect), or
  • manually change the rule each period and lose the audit trail of what rule applied when

Validity periods solve both problems; they give you traceability, automation, and flexibility in a single mechanism.

When the system executes a settlement run for a given period, it applies whichever rule is valid at that point in time. If no rule is valid for the period being settled, the run will typically throw an error.

 

What Settlement History Is

Settlement history is a chronological record of all settlements executed for a cost object. Each time costs accumulated on a object are transferred (settled) to a receiver the system captures a detailed log of that transaction: what was settled, when, to which receiver, and for which period.
The settlement history documents and with this fixes the used settlement rules.

It essentially answers the question: "When has this object been settled and where did the costs go?"


Settlement rule display in app Manage Settlement Rules – Project

The settlement history is displayed with the settlement rules and can be seen either in the Fiori “Manage Settlement Rules – Project” (screenshot above) or directly in e.g. the project master when you navigate to the settlement rule (screenshots below).


Settlement rule display in Project Master

 

Settlement History as a Period-Rule Safeguard

One of the most critical, and often overlooked, functions of settlement history is its role as a consistency guardian within a fiscal period. You can run settlement as many times as needed in a given period: to correct errors, include late postings, or simply re-execute after a failed job. Without a safeguard, each of those re-runs would risk picking up whatever settlement rule happens to be active at that moment, potentially producing contradictory results across runs within the same period.

Settlement history prevents exactly this. The moment a cost object is settled for the first time in a period, the system copies the active distribution rules into the settlement history for that ledger and period and marks them as used. Every subsequent settlement in the same period checks the history first and reapplies those same rules.

The system reinforces this further by locking distribution rules once they have been used in a settlement run. They appear greyed out and cannot be edited directly. If a new rule is created to replace a deleted one, it will only take effect from the next period; the current period's settlement history remains intact.

The only way to change which rule is applied in an already-settled period is to reverse all settlements for that period first - which clears the history entries - then maintain the new rule and re-run settlement. This deliberate friction is by design: it forces a conscious, auditable correction rather than allowing silent mid-period rule changes to distort results.
For additional information about settlement see: SAP Community Blog – Project Settlement with Parallel Ledgers

In practice, this mechanism means that finance and project controllers can run settlement multiple times during period-end close with full confidence: the rule used on the first run is the rule that governs the entire period. The settlement history is not just a log, it is an active control that ensures period-consistent cost allocation from the first run to the last.

Important — Parallel Ledgers
If you are using more than one full ledger (for example IFRS and Local GAAP), settlement postings are ledger-specific. Always check and reconcile history per ledger to see any discrepancies between ledgers.

 

How to Change a Rule Correctly

Once you have read the history, the sequence is:

  1. End-date the existing distribution rule. Set the valid-to date to the last day of the last successfully settled period.
    Or, if you want the change effective immediately, to the last day of the prior period. This change is only possible if no history entry exists for the prior period. Otherwise you need to cancel all settlement runs in the prior period, this will then also delete the history entry.
  2. Create a new distribution rule with the new receiver, effective from the period of the change. If source assignments are in use (source structure), replicate all source assignment lines under the new rule.
  3. Run settlement in test mode for the current period with the new rule in place. Verify receiver and amount. Confirm no residual amounts are still routing to the old receiver.
  4. Execute in update mode.

If you are using processing type Full Settlement and there is still a prior-period open balance, resolve that first: re-run settlement for the prior period, confirm it posts cleanly, then proceed with the current period.

 

The Ledger Dimension

In SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud, Universal Parallel Accounting is always active; settlement values are calculated and posted per ledger. This is why the settlement history is also always updated per ledger.
If your settlement profile uses ledger-specific distribution rules (an optional activation in the settlement profile), each ledger group maintains its own receivers.

When reading history before a rule change, check all active standard ledgers to see for which ledgers settlement rules are used and fixed in the history.
Note also that mass processing can handle several ledgers within one job, but single-object processing must be done ledger by ledger; relevant if you are re-running specific prior periods as part of the correction sequence.

 

Common Mistakes

  • Overlapping validity periods: Creating a new rule without end-dating the old one. The settlement run errors immediately, nothing is silently mis-posted, but it blocks the closing run until resolved.
  • Assuming the new rule "corrects" history: Settlement rules are forward-looking. Changing the receiver does not restate prior-period postings. If costs went to the wrong receiver in prior periods, the correction requires reversal of prior settlement documents, correction of the rule and a re-run.
  • Skipping test mode: Settlement in test mode is free. It shows exactly what will post before you commit.

 

Summary

Settlement history is not an audit annex; it is the prerequisite for any rule change. It tells you when has an object been settled and where did the costs go. Validity periods are the precise mechanism that keeps historical periods stable while allowing future periods to use the new rule.

Read the history first. Set the end date on the old rule. Create the new rule with the correct valid-from. Run in test mode. Resolve any prior-period open balances before proceeding. Then post.

 

Further Information

KBA 3071059 - Change receiver cost center in settlement rule: https://me.sap.com/notes/0003071059

KBA 3364248 - Old settlement rule used even if rule has been updated: https://me.sap.com/notes/0003364248

KAB 3427093 - Reversal with deleted Settlement Rules: https://me.sap.com/notes/0003427093

SAP Help: SAP Help Portal – Distribution Rules for Settlement

SAP Community Blog – Project Settlement with Parallel Ledgers

entry.title: SAP Payment Repository for SAP Cloud ERP
entry.content:
How SAP Is Rethinking Payments in SAP Cloud ERP

Payments are often treated as a solved process. For many organizations, however, the reality is far more complex. Heterogeneous payment landscapes, standalone online banking systems, fragmented processes, and, in the worst cases, associated security risks continue to challenge payment operations. Organizations frequently struggle with limited end-to-end visibility, manual approval structures, and increasing complexity whenever new banks, payment formats, or integration scenarios need to be introduced. As payment ecosystems become more interconnected, real-time, and compliance-driven, these limitations are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

SAP has recognized these challenges and responded with a native SAP Cloud ERP solution that provides the transparency, flexibility, and scalability organizations need to navigate evolving payment requirements. By establishing a centralized foundation for payment processing, it enables companies to streamline operations, strengthen controls, and prepare for future innovation in payments. SAP’s Payment Repository addresses these challenges by introducing a unified and semantically consistent foundation for payment processing, monitoring, and innovation across systems. It is designed to improve transparency, simplify operations, and create a scalable basis for future payment capabilities.

 

 

Why this matters now

Many SAP payment landscapes have grown over time. Different payment sources, bank communication channels, approval models, and format requirements often coexist in parallel. This leads to three recurring challenges.

1. Fragmented monitoring

Payments originate right across the business – in procurement, payroll, treasury, tax and customer-facing processes – and each of those processes has its own owner, its own timing and its own tolerance for delay. Payment status information follows that same split: it stays in the application where the payment happened to be created, rather than in one place where the business can see it. In a typical landscape, a handful of very different business contexts all feed the same bank accounts:

  • Operational supplier spend from accounts payable and procurement, including corporate card spend
  • Treasury-driven flows such as financial transactions, cash sweeps, intercompany settlement and ad-hoc transfers
  • Payroll and other HR payments, with their own confidentiality rules and immovable deadlines
  • Obligation-driven payments such as taxes, dividends and shareholder distributions, or high-volume FI-CA (Contract Accounting) flows
  • Payments initiated outside the core process, for example in external systems connected through SAP BTP
  • Cryptocurrency payments starting to emerge
  • And many more

The underlying challenge is not the number of transaction types, but the absence of one shared view across them. Finance and treasury teams struggle to answer everyday business questions – has this payment reached the bank, why was it rejected, which obligations are still at risk today – without moving between systems and asking the teams that own them. The cost shows up as manual reconciliation effort, exceptions that are found late, and decisions on liquidity and payment risk that are taken with less certainty than they should be.

2. Rigid approval frameworks

Approval processes are often closely linked to bank account structures rather than business context. This can create unnecessary complexity, including:

  • Duplicated approval configuration
  • Manual workarounds
  • Artificial payment batch splitting
  • Limited flexibility for risk-based or functional approvals

In practice, the approval logic may reflect technical constraints more than actual business requirements.

3. Format and integration effort

Each new bank, payment method, country requirement, or file format can add implementation and maintenance effort. Traditional format generation is often source-dependent. This makes it harder to maintain consistent payment semantics across the landscape and increases the cost of integrating new banks or payment innovations.

 

 

What is the Payment Repository?

The Payment Repository provides a central payment data layer based on a unified, ISO 20022-aligned semantic model. It acts as a single source of truth for payment transactions, regardless of their origin. Payments may come from Accounts Payable (AP), Human Resources (HR),Contact Accounting (FI-CA), Advanced Payment Management (APM), Treasury (TRM), or external systems connected through SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP). However, the Payment Repository is more than a storage layer. It is a modular architecture that brings together key payment capabilities in a consistent framework.

Core capabilities

Payment Processor

The Payment Processor handles incoming payment requests and supports the generation of bank-specific payment formats, including formats such as Credit Transfer (pain.001), Bank Protocols (pain.002), Direct debit (pain.008) or Local and country-specific formats. By using a shared semantic foundation, format generation becomes less dependent on the original source application.

Approval Engine

The Approval Engine enables more flexible approval models that are not strictly tied to bank account structures. This supports Functional , Cash  or Power of Attorney approvals using risk-based or business-rule-driven approval flows. This decoupling allows organizations to design approval processes around business requirements rather than technical payment structures. Each of these three approval layers plays a distinct role. Functional approval is performed by experts or managers in the business domain where the payment originates, focused on validating the payment's business data - different approvers apply depending on the origin and purpose of the payment. Cash approval, by contrast, is about optimizing cashflow and liquidity across bank accounts, irrespective of where the payment came from; the approvers here are typically not domain experts but treasury specialists. Finally, POA (Power of Attorney) approval provides the legally required signatory authorization and, since it validates authority rather than content, can in many cases be automated. The approval process itself is also becoming easier to track. An interactive approval history gives requesters and auditors an easy-to-consume audit trail of every step, while a forecast of upcoming approvers helps anticipate how long a payment will still take to clear.

Want to know more?: SAP has described the new Approval Capabilities and concept in two dedicated blogs:

  • Functional Payment Approval - overview and business value
  • setup guide and FAQ.

Approval history: every workflow step, approver is visible in one audit trail.

Payment Format Mapping Engine

The new Payment Format Mapping Engine (which will succeed the DMEE workbench) provides an evolved approach to payment format mapping and generation. Instead of relying heavily on source-specific logic, the format generation process is based on harmonized payment semantics and is with this the single source of truth for payment formats in SAP Cloud ERP. This helps reduce complexity and makes payment formats easier to manage across different banks and scenarios as it also comes with improved usability and easier setup for new banks/formats. It also covers requirements the old workbench struggled with, such as structured address data for ISO 20022

Bank statement and status handling

The Payment Repository also supports the processing and interpretation of bank statements and payment status information, including formats such as camt.052, camt.053, camt.054 or MT940. By harmonizing acknowledgments, rejections, settlement confirmations, and bank feedback, organizations gain a more consistent view of payment status across the lifecycle.

SWIFT Tracker integration

With SWIFT Tracker integration, real-time tracking information from the SWIFT network can be brought directly into the payment lifecycle. This allows treasury and finance teams to trace payments across intermediary banks and view detailed information on fees, processing duration, and exchange rates for each leg of an interbank transaction chain, this gives treasury teams a concrete basis for identifying cost drivers and optimizing their banking relationships - turning payment tracking into a lever for cost savings, not just visibility. Payment tracking becomes a self-service capability rather than a support request.

SWIFT gpi tracking: fees, exchange rates, and status for every intermediary bank in the payment chain, in one view.

End-to-end payment visibility

The key outcome of the Payment Repository is a fully traceable payment journey. A payment can be monitored from initiation through approval, bank transmission, acknowledgment, settlement, and final confirmation - all in one place. For example, a payment created through the Manage Automatic Payments app can be followed end to end. Users can view approval steps, transmission status, bank acknowledgments, and settlement confirmation without switching between multiple applications or systems. This creates a much clearer operational picture for finance, treasury, and shared services teams.

A single supplier payment in the Monitor Payment app: payment method, status, parties, and a full processing history in one screen.

 

 

Business value

The Payment Repository delivers value across four main dimensions.

1. End-to-end transparency

A centralized monitoring layer consolidates approval status, transmission status, bank feedback, settlement information, and posting status. This improves operational control and enables more proactive exception handling through centralized alerts and notifications.

2. Single source of truth

A harmonized payment data model reduces inconsistencies between systems and applications. This improves reporting, analytics, auditability, and process governance. Instead of reconciling different payment views, teams can work from one consistent source of payment information.

3. Simplified bank connectivity and format management

The shared semantic layer reduces dependency on source systems. This can lower the effort required to onboard new banks, introduce new payment formats, or adapt to changing regulatory and market requirements.

4. Faster access to payment innovation

New capabilities can be introduced through the repository layer without redesigning each source process. Examples include:

  • SWIFT Tracker
  • Verification of Payee
  • Real-time payment scenarios
  • Enhanced payment status services
  • Future compliance or regulatory requirements

SAP is also positioning the Payment Repository as a foundation for AI-driven use cases. With a unified payment data model, users could eventually ask natural-language questions such as: “Was invoice 4711 paid?”  “Which payments were rejected today?”  “Which high-value payments are still awaiting approval?”

 

 

Extending the model: a cloud-based SAP Payment Factory

The Payment Repository's relevance is not limited to organizations that have already fully moved to SAP Cloud ERP. SAP is also positioning it as the foundation of a cloud-based Payment Factory: a central payment factory with an in-house bank, running on SAP Cloud ERP, that can be extended with Treasury and Risk Management and Cash Management.

This central factory can act as the payment hub for feeder systems that have not yet moved to the cloud - including S/4HANA On-Premise, S/4HANA Private Cloud Edition, SAP ERP, and even external, non-SAP systems. Bank connectivity is handled centrally through SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity, so on-premise or private-cloud landscapes can benefit from Cloud ERP payment innovations without first having to migrate entirely.

For organizations planning a multi-year transformation, this matters in practice: it offers a step-by-step path towards SAP Cloud ERP rather than an all-or-nothing migration, letting treasury modernize its payment operations ahead of a broader system move.

 

 

Industry perspective: KPMG on the Payment Repository and its value

 

Jean-Michele Szczecina – Senior Manager at KPMG Switzerland: We are pleased to see SAP’s continued investment in Treasury capabilities. In our view, the Payment Repository concept addresses an important need for greater transparency across complex payment processes by providing a centralized view of payment-related information. Combined with process flexibility that can be aligned with different business requirements, it offers an additional option for organizations evaluating their future payment architecture, including transitions from SAP Bank Communication Management (BCM).

Adrian Matys – Senior Manager at KPMG Switzerland: In our experience, the Payment Repository in SAP Cloud ERP introduces a centralized approach to managing payment-related data and processes. It offers organizations additional options for monitoring and managing payments within SAP Cloud ERP and may help support greater transparency and consistency across payment workflows. In combination with SAP Advanced Payment Management, the repository can be complemented by capabilities such as batching, validation, and screening, depending on the specific business and compliance requirements of an organization.

From transparency to value

Both perspectives point beyond the repository itself. Transparency is the entry ticket, not the destination - once payments flow through one harmonized layer, the question becomes what you build on top of it. That is where the payment factory and the in-house bank come in: the operating model that turns a central payment layer into measurable value. KPMG examined what it delivers in practice, and three observations tend to surprise.

  • The cheapest payment is the one that never reaches a bank. Payments and collections on behalf of subsidiaries, settled across in-house bank accounts, remove fees, FX spreads and bank connections from the equation instead of negotiating them down.
  • Idle cash is a bigger prize than transaction cost. Internal accounts, cash pooling and internal financing let treasury fund its own subsidiaries rather than leaving liquidity buffers parked in local accounts around the world.
  • Control becomes structural rather than procedural. One approval framework, central screening, one audit trail across every entity - the payment that never goes wrong outweighs the fee discussion.

Together, that turns treasury into a genuine internal bank: the control mechanisms of a financial institution, without its regulatory burden - resting on exactly the harmonized payment data the Payment Repository provides.

What to know more? here is the link to access the complete analysis and Whitepaper from KPMG : Unlocking Liquidity, Control and Efficiency: SAP In-House Banking in Practice

 

 

The Payment Repository impact – moving from payment monitoring to payment orchestration

Looking ahead, the Payment Repository is moving beyond centralized monitoring toward becoming an orchestration layer for payments in heterogeneous landscapes. One of the most important developments is the move toward unified payment processing. Approval, execution, format generation, bank communication, and status handling can be managed within a more consistent framework instead of being distributed across multiple disconnected components.

Another key direction is the harmonization of bank feedback. By standardizing how acknowledgments, rejections, settlement confirmations, and tracking updates are interpreted, organizations can gain better transparency without adding integration complexity. The approval architecture is also more flexible now. By decoupling approvals from bank accounts, organizations can align workflows with business rules, risk profiles, payment types, or organizational responsibilities. This reduces operational overhead and improves governance. At the same time, the Payment Repository is becoming a central integration layer for bank connectivity and payment innovation. The repository provides a consistent foundation for future capabilities.

On the monitoring side, multiple apps are still often required to identify the execution status of a payment from different sources. The Payment Repository bridges this with deeper SWIFT Tracker integration, native integration of payment sources, and dedicated situations handling so that exceptions are surfaced proactively rather than discovered by chance.

Finally, the unified data model creates a stronger basis for intelligent and automated payment operations that is planned on the SAP roadmap. Complete lifecycle visibility opens the door to scenarios such as:

  • Predictive exception handling
  • Automated status interpretation
  • AI-supported payment monitoring
  • Natural-language interaction with payment data
  • Proactive alerting for delayed, rejected, or high-risk payments

 

 

What's on the Roadmap

SAP's roadmap extends the same shifts described above: approvals that follow business rules, formats generated from one semantic model, and monitoring that surfaces problems instead of waiting to be asked. Four entries are worth watching.

Signatory-governed payment approvals: Approvals derived from the signatory rights and powers of attorney held in Bank Account Management, so authorization is enforced by the system rather than rebuilt in a workflow. [Link]

Payment Risk Insights Agent: An AI agent that watches the payment flow and flags what deserves attention: unusual beneficiaries, amounts out of pattern, payments at risk of missing their value date. [Link]

Verification of Payee (VoP): A beneficiary name check before the payment leaves, mandatory for euro credit transfers in the EU and every payment source inherits it from the repository layer. [Link]

SAP Universal Payment Format: One harmonized format definition across banks and countries, so a new format becomes a variant rather than a project. [Link]

 

 

Closing perspective

By combining harmonized data, decoupled approvals, centralized monitoring, and simplified integration, it helps finance and treasury teams move away from fragmented execution and toward a more controlled, scalable, and insight-driven payment process.  For organizations planning their SAP Cloud ERP implementation or already using it, the Payment Repository is more than a technical enhancement. It represents a structural shift in how payments are managed, monitored, and connected across the enterprise - laying the foundation for a more transparent and intelligent payment operation going forward.

entry.title: Wenn Finance mehr sieht als Automatisierung
entry.content:
Für die Sonnenfinsternis reiste ich nach Nordspanien. Ich hatte die Bilder im Kopf, die wir alle kennen: Dunkelheit, die schwarze Scheibe vor der Sonne, die leuchtende Korona. Spektakulär – aber auch ein wenig abstrakt.
 
Und dann stand ich dort, gemeinsam mit vielen anderen Menschen, und erlebte etwas völlig anderes. Es wurde nicht einfach nur dunkel. Die ganze Umgebung veränderte sich: das Licht, die Farben, die Temperatur, die Geräusche, die Stimmung. Menschen wurden still. Die Landschaft wirkte plötzlich fremd und zugleich intensiver. Der Moment war magischer, größer und unmittelbarer, als ich erwartet hatte.
 
Das Beeindruckende war nicht die Korona allein. Das Beeindruckende war der Kontext: die Landschaft, die Menschen, die Stille und die Veränderung des gesamten Augenblicks. Für mich ist das ein treffendes Bild für AI in Finance.
 
Automatisierung, die sichtbare Korona:
Wenn wir heute über AI in Finance sprechen, beginnen wir meist mit klaren Erwartungen: schneller abschließen, weniger manuelle Arbeit, bessere Forecasts, weniger Fehler. Das ist wichtig. Es ist sichtbar, messbar und schafft echten Mehrwert. AI kann beispielsweise Buchungen vorbereiten, Abgrenzungen vorschlagen, Anomalien erkennen, Abstimmungen beschleunigen oder offene Forderungen priorisieren. Damit gewinnen Finance-Teams Zeit und können sich stärker auf Analyse, Steuerung und Entscheidungen konzentrieren. Diese Effekte sind unsere Korona: sichtbar, überzeugend und wichtig. Aber sie sind alles.
 
Der Kontext macht den Unterschied
Im Finance sehen wir jeden Tag Signale: eine Rechnung, die nicht bezahlt wird. Eine Buchung, die nicht zum erwarteten Muster passt. Eine Änderung im Steuerrecht. Eine Beschaffung, die vom Vertrag abweicht. Eine Bewegung im Cash Forecast. Eine Richtlinie, die überprüft werden muss. Jedes dieser Ereignisse ist zunächst nur ein Signal. Seine Bedeutung entsteht erst aus dem Kontext. Welche Gesellschaft ist betroffen? Welche Policy gilt? Welche Risiken entstehen? Welche weiteren Prozesse hängen daran? Wer muss entscheiden? Und welche Handlung ist jetzt richtig?
 
Genau hier liegt die Chance von AI in Finance: nicht nur Informationen schneller bereitzustellen, sondern Kontext zu verbinden, Relevanz sichtbar zu machen und Arbeit kontrolliert voranzubringen.
 
Eine überfällige Rechnung ist dafür ein gutes Beispiel. Die Information allein reicht nicht aus. Finance muss verstehen: Gibt es einen offenen Disput? Welche Zahlungshistorie hat der Kunde? Wie wirkt sich die Forderung auf Liquidität und Cash Forecast aus? Gibt es weitere offene Posten oder eine Zusage zur Zahlung? Und was ist die sinnvollste nächste Maßnahme?
 
AI kann diese Informationen zusammenführen, Prioritäten sichtbar machen und Handlungsmöglichkeiten vorschlagen. Der Mensch entscheidet – aber auf einer besseren Informationsbasis und mit deutlich weniger manueller Recherche.
 
Das gilt auch für den Financial Close. Es geht nicht nur darum, einen Abschluss schneller zu erstellen. Es geht darum, Auffälligkeiten früh zu erkennen, mögliche Ursachen einzuordnen, die richtigen Personen einzubinden und nachvollziehbar zu machen, was geprüft oder entschieden werden muss.
 
Die Zukunft von Finance liegt deshalb nicht in einer Black Box, die Entscheidungen ersetzt. Sie liegt in einer intelligenten Zusammenarbeit zwischen Menschen, Daten, Prozessen und AI.
 
AI übernimmt die zeitaufwendige Suche, Analyse und Vorbereitung. Sie kann Muster erkennen, Zusammenhänge herstellen und nächste Schritte anstoßen. Finance-Expertinnen und -Experten bringen dagegen das ein, was in komplexen Situationen entscheidend bleibt: Erfahrung, Urteilsvermögen, Verantwortlichkeit und Verständnis für das Geschäft.
 
Damit das funktioniert, braucht AI einen verlässlichen Rahmen: hochwertige Daten, klare Prozesse, definierte Rollen, Berechtigungen und Governance. Gerade in Finance müssen Empfehlungen nachvollziehbar sein und sich innerhalb von Richtlinien, Kontrollen und regulatorischen Anforderungen bewegen.
 
Die entscheidende Frage lautet daher nicht nur: Welche Tätigkeiten können wir automatisieren? Die spannendere Frage ist: Wie verändert sich Finance, wenn Daten, Prozesse, Regeln und Expertise im richtigen Moment zusammenkommen?
 
Mit SAP Business AI geht es nicht nur darum, die sichtbare Korona der Automatisierung zu erreichen. Es geht darum, den gesamten Kontext von Finance zu verstehen – damit aus Daten bessere Entscheidungen und aus Entscheidungen wirksame, kontrollierte Handlungen werden.

entry.title: Pain Points in Sustainable Finance
entry.content:
Over the last few years, sustainability has moved from the sidelines to the CFO agenda. 

That sounds obvious now, but regulatory pressure is increasing, investors are asking tougher questions, and companies are expected to demonstrate measurable progress rather than simply publish reports. Finance teams have become central players in this shift. 

The biggest challenge isn't proving sustainability matters. It's making it operational. 

While sustainability has become a business priority, many finance teams are running into the same challenge: It's easy to agree sustainability matters. It's much harder to embed it into the way the business actually runs. 

With that, three pain points stand out.

Pain Point #1: Sustainability Data Is Everywhere, But Rarely Connected 

Most organizations don't have a sustainability ambition problem. They have a data problem.  

Financial data lives in one system. Operational data lives in another. Sustainability data often lives somewhere else entirely. Bringing everything together for reporting, planning, and analysis can require significant manual effort. 

The result is that teams spend more time reconciling information than acting on it. 

This is where SAP's ecosystem becomes especially important. Finance, operations, supply chain, and sustainability teams can't make informed decisions when data is scattered across multiple systems. By bringing these data sources together, SAP helps organizations establish a shared foundation for sustainability and business decision-making, reducing manual reconciliation and increasing confidence in the numbers being used. 

Pain Point #2: Reporting Requirements Keep Expanding 

A few years ago, many sustainability programs focused primarily on emissions reporting. Today, expectations are considerably higher. 

Organizations are managing evolving disclosure requirements, increased scrutiny around auditability, and rising demand for product-level carbon footprints. 

The challenge for finance teams isn't simply generating another report. Rather, it is creating a reporting process that is repeatable, trustworthy, and scalable as requirements continue to evolve. 

This challenge underscores the value of SAP's integrated sustainability portfolio. As regulations and disclosure requirements continue to evolve, organizations need more than another reporting tool. They need sustainability processes embedded into the systems already used to manage finance, supply chain, and operations. SAP's approach helps organizations build a reporting foundation that can scale as requirements become more complex. 

Pain Point #3: Demonstrating Business Value 

Most organizations can measure sustainability activities, while fewer can clearly connect them to business outcomes. 

Finance leaders are being asked to justify investments, prioritize initiatives, and demonstrate value. That means sustainability programs need to show how they contribute to cost reduction, operational efficiency, risk management, resilience, or growth. 

Without that connection, sustainability can feel like another reporting requirement rather than a business driver. 

That's why the conversation is increasingly shifting from: "How do we report sustainability?" to "How do we use sustainability to make better business decisions?" 

Perhaps most importantly, SAP is helping organizations bridge the gap between sustainability performance and business performance. When sustainability data is connected to financial and operational outcomes, leaders can evaluate trade-offs, prioritize investments, and measure impact with greater confidence. That's when sustainability starts to move from a cost of compliance to a driver of business value. 

What Pain Points Are You Seeing? 

As sustainability becomes more embedded in finance, new challenges continue to emerge around data, reporting, planning, and demonstrating business value. 

If you're seeing a different pain point in your organization, let me know. I'd be happy to explore it in a future post and take a closer look at how SAP solutions look to address it.

entry.title: SAP Joule for Beginners: Where to Start and What You Really Need
entry.content:
Recently, I had the opportunity to attend an SAP chapter meeting in Newtown Square, Pennsylvania. The agenda was AI focused. An attendee asked a practical question: "Can Joule help me find information about purchase orders or explain financial transactions without navigating multiple SAP screens?" The discussion highlighted a common misconception. Many newcomers assume they need custom AI development, AI Core, or Generative AI Hub before receiving any value from SAP AI. In reality, many organizations can start by enabling standard Joule capabilities delivered by SAP and allowing users to interact with business data through natural-language questions. This example reinforced my belief that organizations should focus first on learning the standard capabilities before investing in advanced AI architectures.

What exactly is Joule, and where do I start?

SAP has introduced several AI-related services and acronyms over the past few years. For a newcomer, it can be difficult to understand which components are required, which are optional, and which are intended only for developers and business.

This blog is intended for the naive first-time SAP user, architect, or project lead who simply wants to activate and use standard Joule capabilities, without immediately diving into custom AI development.

What Is Joule?

Joule is SAP's AI copilot and AI assistant designed to bring AI capabilities directly into SAP business applications. As artificial intelligence has evolved rapidly, SAP has expanded its portfolio with a growing set of AI-powered products and services. Many of these offerings include the terms "Joule" or "AI" in their names, which can make the landscape confusing for newcomers. So whether it is Rule based AI (Condition based), Machine learning AI (Algorithms like linear regression, time series analysis etc.), Generative AI (coding assistance, knowledge management etc.), Retrieval augmented AI (Q&A) or with latest AI evolution on Agentic AI (Workflows etc.) and Autonomous Agents (E2E business process execution etc.), the SAP AI ecosystem can appear overwhelming when viewed as a collection of acronyms and components. However, when approached incrementally, the journey becomes much more manageable. Think of Joule as the front door to SAP's AI ecosystem.

Understanding the SAP AI Landscape

Component

Purpose

Target Audience

Conversational AI interface

When I first started researching Joule, I found myself trying to understand whether every item in this table was required. The good news is that if your goal is simply to use SAP-delivered Joule capabilities, you do not need to implement every component from day one.

My Recommendation for Activating Base Joule

For organizations looking to take their first step, I recommend focusing on three areas:

Step 1: Set Up SAP BTP

SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) is the foundation for nearly all modern SAP innovation, including Joule.

Before anything else, ensure:

  • There is a BTP tenant
  • Global Account is set up
  • Sub Account is set up Note: This is critical as Services are activated in one subaccount while the testing or changes are done in another subaccount.
  • Identity and authentication are configured
  • Connectivity exists between BTP and SAP applications
  • Appropriate user roles are assigned

Based on one of the sessions during the chapter meeting it was explained that this is often the largest hurdle. The technology itself is not necessarily difficult, but understanding subaccounts, entitlements, destinations, and identity services can be confusing when starting from scratch.

My recommendation: Don't begin with AI. Begin with BTP readiness. If the BTP foundation is not established, the AI journey will be significantly more difficult.

Step 2: Activate Joule

After the BTP environment is ready, Joule can be enabled according to SAP's activation guidance.

At a high level, organizations should:

  • Verify licensing requirements
  • Use weblink: Discovery Center and review the list of Joule services/enablement. Note:  You can find all SAP AI updates.  
  • Enable Joule services
  • Configure system integrations
  • Assign user authorizations
  • Test access with pilot users

This is where many organizations become overwhelmed because they immediately start discussing large language models, Agentic AI, Autonomous AI, workflows, custom copilots.

My recommendation: For the first implementation the goal should be adoption and learning, not perfection.

  • Focus on getting the base Joule experience working for a small group of users before pursuing advanced AI scenarios or custom development. Users can interact with Joule through natural-language prompts, allowing them to access information and business insights from supported SAP applications without navigating multiple screens.

Step 3: Use Standard SAP-Delivered Skills

This is the step many organizations skip. Instead of immediately building custom AI solutions, begin by exploring SAP-delivered skills that already exist in supported business applications.

Benefits include:

  • Faster deployment
  • Lower risk
  • SAP-supported functionality Note: SAP manages the large language models, monitoring, fixes etc. 
  • Clearer business value realization

In my experience, once users begin interacting with Joule through natural language, they often discover other use cases. 

Only after gaining practical experience should organizations consider custom development through Joule Studio, AI Core, or Generative AI Hub.

When Should You Consider Advanced AI Components?

  • Once standard Joule capabilities are set up.
  • Developers and Business users are using the base version and are familiar with UI Navigation and how responses are structured
  • The base Joule version and SAP standard skills are delivering value 

Lessons Learned

Reflecting on the conversations at the Newtown Square SAP chapter meeting, my biggest takeaway is that many SAP professionals are asking the same question:

Where do I start?

  1. Establish SAP BTP foundation
  2. Activate base Joule
  3. Use SAP-delivered skills
  4. Learn from real business usage
  5. Expand into custom AI only when there is a proven business need

 

Start with the SAP-delivered capabilities that already exist today. Build your BTP foundation, activate Joule, explore standard skills, and learn from real business usage before investing in advanced AI development.

If you are wondering whether your organization is "late" to the Joule journey, don't worry. Based on the conversations I had at the SAP chapter meeting many organizations are still evaluating where to begin. The most important step is simply getting started.

entry.title: SAP RAR Transformation from CIP to OIP: Architecture Evolution, SD Integration, and Implementation
entry.content:
🚀SAP S/4HANA RAR: Transforming Classic Inbound Processing (CIP) to Optimized Inbound Processing (OIP)

Recently, I had the opportunity to work on a CIP-to-OIP transformation for a business process integrated with SAP SD and SAP Revenue Accounting and Reporting (RAR).

🎯The objective: Move from the traditional CIP model to real-time processing while minimizing the impact on existing business processes.

In this blog, I share my hands-on experience implementing OIP for business process integrated with SAP SD and SAP RAR.

I highlight the below key aspects:

🏗️ Architecture changes and processing flow
⚙️Key differences between CIP and OIP
🗄️ Database impacts
🔧Enhancement adjustments
📊Monitoring differences
✅Implementation challenges and lessons learned
 
The blog should help SAP RAR consultants, architects, and developers understand what changes, what remains unchanged, and what should be considered before starting an OIP implementation. OIP processes Revenue Accounting Items synchronously and eliminates the traditional transfer and processing job framework used in CIP.
 
Introduction

With SAP S/4HANA, SAP introduced Optimized Contract Management (OCM) and Optimized Inbound Processing (OIP) to simplify and modernize Revenue Accounting and Reporting (RAR). OIP represents a fundamental shift in how Revenue Accounting Items (RAIs) are created and processed. Instead of relying on queues and batch jobs, OIP processes RAIs in real time during document creation. SAP positions OIP as the optimized successor to Classic Inbound Processing (CIP) within modern S/4HANA RAR landscapes. 

Optimized Inbound Processing (OIP) is one of the most significant innovations introduced in S/4 HANA SAP Revenue Accounting and Reporting (RAR). Unlike Classic Inbound Processing (CIP), which relies on background jobs and multi-step processing, OIP enables real-time creation and processing of Revenue Accounting Items (RAIs) directly when operational documents are posted.

This article summarizes the key findings from the implementation project.

Understanding the Existing CIP Architecture

In the traditional CIP architecture, Revenue Accounting Item processing occurs in multiple stages:

  1. Sales Order (RAR Relevant) is created
  2. SD Billing Document is created.
  3. RAI is generated in Raw or Processable status .
  4. Program FARR_RAI_TRANSFER converts Raw RAIs to Processable RAIs.
  5. Program FARR_RAI_PROC processes the RAI.
  6. Revenue Accounting Contracts and POBs are created in OCM.
  7. Revenue Recognition and GL postings are executed.

This architecture introduces a processing delay because RAIs depend on scheduled background jobs before becoming available for Revenue Accounting processing. The user must also monitor transfer and processing jobs, adding operational overhead. Revenue Accounting inbound processing traditionally uses processing statuses and monitoring frameworks for RAI lifecycle management.

What Changes with OIP?

The biggest difference is that OIP processes RAIs synchronously. 

OIP is SAP's new real-time method for creating Revenue Accounting Items (RAIs) inside SAP RAR (Revenue Accounting and Reporting).

When an SD Billing document is saved, RAIs are immediately processed without requiring:

  • FARR_RAI_TRANSFER
  • FARR_RAI_PROC
  • Scheduled batch jobs
  • Queue-based intermediate processing

The flow becomes:

SD Sales Order → SD Billing Document → Processed RAI → Revenue Accounting Contract → Revenue Recognition

This significantly reduces latency between the operational transaction and Revenue Accounting processing. Instead of waiting for background jobs, contract creation and downstream processing can start instantly.

Key Architecture Changes

Before (CIP)

  • Two-step processing model
  • Queue and batch job dependent
  • Multiple RAI status transitions
  • Monitoring via FARR_RAI_MON
  • Legacy /1RA/* tables

After (OIP)

  • Single-step real-time processing
  • No transfer job required
  • Immediate Revenue Contract creation
  • Monitoring through Fiori application "Manage Revenue Accounting Items"
  • New FARR_D_* table framework

The simplification is not only technical but also operational. Support teams no longer need to monitor multiple inbound processing jobs throughout the day.

Changes in RAI Status Management

One important behavioral change is the RAI status model.

CIP Status Flow

Raw → Processable → Processed

OIP Status Flow

Processed

or

Postponed → Processed

In OIP, if required information is unavailable during processing, the RAI is placed in Postponed status rather than remaining in intermediary technical statuses. Once the missing information is provided, the RAI can be reprocessed.

This results in a significantly cleaner operational model.

Database Table Changes

One of the most important technical impacts of OIP is the replacement of classic RAI tables.

 


For organizations with custom reports, CDS views, custom transactions, or direct table reads, this is often the most significant migration activity because all table dependencies must be reviewed and redesigned.

Monitoring and Error Handling After OIP

The operational support model also changes.

CIP Monitoring

  • FARR_RAI_MON - Revenue Accounting Item Monitor
  • Transfer job monitoring (FARR_RAI_TRANS - Transfer RAI's from Raw (0) to Processable (2) )
  • Processing job monitoring (FARR_RAI_PROC - Process Revenue Accounting Items)

OIP Monitoring

  • Fiori App: Manage Revenue Accounting Items
  • Postponed Revenue Accounting Item processing (Transaction code: FARR_REPR_PPRAI - Reprocess Postponed RAI )
  • Real-time status visibility

The monitoring experience becomes much more business-friendly because users can directly analyze and reprocess postponed items without depending heavily on technical batch-job execution.

Lessons Learned

1. Mixed CIP and OIP scenarios require significantly more custom code adaptation than initially expected

One assumption we made at the beginning was that the transition effort would primarily focus on replacing CIP-specific objects with their OIP equivalents. In reality, the biggest challenge was supporting business processes that relied on extensive custom logic while keeping some processes on CIP and others on OIP during the transition period. This created additional complexity in custom programs, enhancements, and reports.

For example, several custom reports were built on legacy Revenue Accounting tables such as /1RA* tables and had to be redesigned to consume the new FARR_D* data model because a simple table replacement was not sufficient. If we were to repeat the project, we would perform a more detailed dependency analysis of custom developments at the very beginning and identify mixed CIP/OIP process impacts before defining the migration approach.

2. End-user readiness for the new monitoring approach was more critical than anticipated

We initially focused on the technical migration activities and underestimated the impact of changes to daily business operations. With OIP, users can no longer rely on transaction FARR_RAI_MON, which many support and business users used to quickly identify Revenue Accounting Items and navigate to contracts. Instead, they must work with the Fiori app Manage Revenue Accounting Items, where accessing related contracts often requires additional navigation steps through hyperlinks.

This change affected troubleshooting efficiency immediately after go-live. Looking back, we would introduce hands-on training and updated support procedures much earlier in the project to ensure users are comfortable with the new Fiori-based monitoring process before the cutover.

Walkthrough of Optimized Inbound Processing (OIP) in SAP RAR

Determine IP Version

BRFplus for Inbound Processing
